descriptions.value: The legendary rivalry of Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin produced five clashes on the Kawanakajima plain between 1553 and 1564; the fourth, in 1561, was the bloodiest and most celebrated in samurai lore. The name covers five campaigns in the same district between 1553 and 1564. Only the fourth, in 1561, was a major battle, fought around Hachimanbara. The marker is the Kawanakajima plain as a whole; the sites of the 1561 battle and the 1564 standoff are drawn while this entry is open. Several separate engagements are combined in this entry.

Oda Nobuhide, father of Oda Nobunaga, is recorded as defeating Imagawa Yoshimoto in Mikawa, asserting Oda strength along the road his son would later make famous, though some historians hold this first Azukizaka battle to be a later fabrication, since the Imagawa push into eastern Mikawa is dated only from 1543. Whether this battle happened at all is doubted. The historian Owada Tetsuo dates the Imagawa advance into eastern Mikawa to 1543 or later, which leaves a battle in 1542 without an occasion. The second battle at Azukizaka, in 1548, is well attested. Whether this event took place is doubted.

descriptions.value: Oda Nobunaga's attack destroyed an army ten times his size and killed the great Imagawa Yoshimoto, the upset that announced Nobunaga to the realm. How he did it is disputed: the famous story of a hidden flanking march under cover of a storm is now doubted by many historians, who read the earliest chronicle as describing a frontal assault. Two localities claim the site. Toyoake holds the nationally designated historic site, and Nagoya's Midori Ward keeps a rival battlefield park about 1 km to the west. The marker sits on the designated site; both candidates are drawn while this entry is open. How the attack was made is disputed too (see the text).

descriptions.value: The clash where Oda–Tokugawa arquebusiers, fighting from behind field palisades, broke Takeda Katsuyori's assaults. Long celebrated as the dawn of gunpowder warfare in Japan, though modern scholarship rejects both the 'three-stage volley' of 3,000 guns and the image of a massed Takeda cavalry charge.

Uesugi Kenshin's last major campaign, an Oda relief army under Shibata Katsuie was caught withdrawing across the flooded Tedori River and mauled. Nobunaga was not present, and the battle's scale and outcome rest on thin evidence: the Shinchō Kōki records the sortie but no battle. The chronicle of Nobunaga's side records a withdrawal but no battle, while Uesugi Kenshin's own letter claims a pursuit and a victory. Historians accept that the armies met; the scale and character of the clash are disputed.

descriptions.value: The coup that killed Oda Nobunaga: his trusted general Akechi Mitsuhide turned his army on the lightly guarded temple where Nobunaga lodged, ending the career of the man who had nearly unified Japan. The marker is the temple as it stood in 1582. Excavation has confirmed that the compound filled one block about 120 m square, bounded by Rokkaku, Nishinotōin, Shijō-bōmon (today Takoyakushi) and Aburanokōji streets; the block is drawn while this entry is open. The present Honnō-ji, rebuilt in 1591, stands 1.4 km away.
Eleven days after killing Nobunaga, Akechi Mitsuhide was crushed by Hideyoshi at Yamazaki, the battle that made Hideyoshi heir to Nobunaga's power.

names.toponym: Ichi-no-Tani, Suma, Settsu Province (modern Suma-ku, Kobe)

descriptions.value: Yoshitsune's most famous stroke. While Noriyori's main army struck the Taira line at Ikuta Shrine to the east, Yoshitsune took a detachment of about a hundred riders over the mountains behind the fortress and fell on the defenders' rear, throwing the Taira into rout. It is the setting of the death of the young flute-player Taira no Atsumori at the hands of Kumagai Naozane. The famous descent down the cliffs (sakaotoshi) is placed by rival traditions above Ichi-no-Tani at Tekkaisan, or about 5 km east at Hiyodorigoe; some historians also question where Ichi-no-Tani itself lay. The marker is the conventional battlefield at Ichi-no-Tani; both descent sites are drawn while this entry is open.

descriptions.value: The naval battle that ended the Genpei War. In the swift tidal narrows of the Shimonoseki Strait the two fleets met; as the tide turned and Taira allies defected, their cause collapsed. The grandmother of the six-year-old Emperor Antoku leapt into the sea with him rather than be captured, and with the Taira annihilated the way lay open to the Kamakura shogunate. A naval battle fought in the Kanmon (Shimonoseki) strait, drawn as a line along the strait. The marker is the Dan-no-ura shore. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Uji–Seta river crossings, approaches to Kyoto (modern Kyoto), coordinates approximate

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The retired Emperor Go-Toba's bid to overthrow the Kamakura shogunate and restore direct imperial rule. The Hōjō regency's eastern armies crushed the imperial forces at the river crossings south of Kyoto and took the capital within weeks, sealing warrior dominance over the court for the rest of the medieval age. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Hakata Bay, Chikuzen Province (modern Fukuoka), coordinates approximate

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The first Mongol invasion. A Yuan–Goryeo fleet landed in Hakata Bay and shook the Japanese with massed formations, poisoned arrows and exploding bombs, but re-embarked at nightfall and was scattered by a storm, sparing Kyūshū and prompting Japan to build a defensive stone wall along the bay. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Hakata Bay & the defensive stone wall, Chikuzen Province (modern Fukuoka), coordinates approximate

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The second and far larger Mongol invasion. Two huge fleets converged on Kyūshū but were held off the new stone wall along Hakata Bay for weeks; after withdrawing west to Imari Bay, off Takashima, the anchored armada was annihilated by a great typhoon, remembered as the kamikaze, the 'divine wind', ending Kublai Khan's attempts to conquer Japan. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Chihaya Castle site, on the western slopes of Mt. Kongō, Kawachi Province (modern Chihayaakasaka, Osaka)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 千早城の戦い (Siege of Chihaya)

descriptions.value: Kusunoki Masashige's legendary defense of the small mountain fortress of Chihaya against a vast Hōjō army. His ingenious guerrilla tricks, logs, boulders and feints, held the castle for months, tying down the shogunate's strength and emboldening Emperor Go-Daigo's supporters to rise across the country. A designated national historic site (1934). The marker is on the castle remains, not on the summit of Mt. Kongō.

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Nitta Yoshisada's assault on the shogunal capital. By tradition he turned the city's coastal defenses by leading his army across the beach at Inamuragasaki at an unusually low tide; Kamakura fell amid heavy fighting, and the last Hōjō regent Takatoki and hundreds of his kin took their own lives, ending nearly 150 years of Kamakura rule and opening the way to the Kenmu Restoration.

names.toponym: Mouth of the Kizu River, Osaka Bay

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Two massive naval engagements. The Mōri initially broke the Oda blockade of Ishiyama Hongan-ji, prompting Nobunaga to build six great iron-reinforced atakebune, which beat back the Mōri fleet in 1578 but still could not seal off the fortress. Two naval battles at the same river mouth, in 1576 and 1578, are combined in this entry. Several separate engagements are combined in this entry.

names.toponym: Hara Castle, Shimabara Peninsula, Hizen Province (modern Nagasaki Prefecture)

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The largest uprising of the Edo period: overtaxed peasants and persecuted Christians on the Shimabara Peninsula and Amakusa Islands rose under the teenage Amakusa Shirō, holding out at Hara Castle against a vast shogunate army. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Toba and Fushimi, south of Kyoto

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Though outnumbered three to one, the modernized, Imperial-bannered Satsuma–Chōshū army routed the shogunate forces south of Kyoto, opening the Boshin War and turning the conflict into a legitimist crusade against the Tokugawa.

After Edo surrendered peacefully, the die-hard Shōgitai held out at Kan'ei-ji temple in Ueno. Ōmura Masujirō's Imperial troops, using Armstrong guns, crushed them in one day, cementing Imperial control of the new capital.

names.toponym: Tsuruga Castle, Aizuwakamatsu, Mutsu Province (modern Fukushima Prefecture)

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The bloodiest campaign of the Boshin War. The Tokugawa-loyalist Aizu domain made a desperate stand at Tsuruga Castle; the tragedy of the teenage Byakkotai, who took their own lives believing the castle had fallen, became a national legend.

The last stand of the Tokugawa cause. Naval officer Enomoto Takeaki and former Shinsengumi vice-commander Hijikata Toshizō held the star-shaped Goryōkaku fortress in Hokkaido as the short-lived 'Ezo Republic,' until Imperial forces overwhelmed them in mid-1869. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: A decade-long conflict that began as a shogunal succession dispute and engulfed Kyoto, splitting the great houses into Eastern (Hosokawa) and Western (Yamana) armies. The capital was reduced to ashes and the Muromachi shogunate's authority shattered, the conventional opening of the Sengoku 'Warring States' age. An eleven-year war fought across the city of Kyoto and beyond. The marker is in Nishijin, named after the Western Army's camp. The shaded area is the province of Yamashiro, the nearest unit for which the atlas has a sourced boundary; the atlas has no boundary for the medieval city itself. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it. Area: the province of Yamashiro (whole units, an approximation).

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Retaliation for the killing of an English merchant at Namamugi (1862), a British squadron bombarded Kagoshima. Both sides claimed victory, but Satsuma drew the real lesson, that 'expel the barbarians' was futile, and turned to Western arms.

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: After Chōshū fired on foreign shipping in the strait to 'expel the barbarians,' a four-nation fleet returned in 1864 and smashed its forts, teaching Chōshū the same hard lesson Satsuma had learned at Kagoshima. Several separate bombardments in 1863 and 1864 are combined in this entry. Several separate engagements are combined in this entry.

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Seeking to reverse its loss of influence, Chōshū marched on the Kyoto palace to 'rescue' the Emperor. Aizu and Satsuma troops beat the assault back at the Hamaguri Gate; the defeated Chōshū force set Kyoto ablaze, beginning with the Takatsukasa mansion; the resulting fire destroyed some 28,000 houses.

names.toponym: The Chōshū borders (Suō / Nagato), four fronts around Yamaguchi

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The shogunate's second attempt to crush Chōshū ended in humiliating failure: Chōshū's small, modern, rifle-armed force defeated the vast but antiquated Tokugawa coalition on every front. The defeat doomed the shogunate. Fought on four fronts around the borders of Chōshū. The marker is one inland point; the shaded area is Chōshū's two provinces, Suō and Nagato. Two of the fronts lay just outside them, in Iwami and Buzen. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it. Area: Suō and Nagato, the two provinces of Chōshū (whole units, an approximation).

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The first great samurai revolt: a Kantō warrior overruns eight eastern provinces and proclaims himself a 'New Emperor,' shocking the Heian court. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Iyo Province & the Seto Inland Sea (modern Ehime)

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: A court official turned pirate king raises the Inland Sea against Kyoto, the western half of the twin revolts that revealed the warriors' rising power. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Mutsu Province, the Kitakami valley (modern Iwate)

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: A twelve-year war in the far north that made the Minamoto the pre-eminent warrior house of eastern Japan. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Traditional site of the Kanezawa stockade, Kanazawa Park, Dewa Province (modern Yokote, Akita); not confirmed by excavation

descriptions.value: Minamoto Yoshiie intervenes in a northern clan's feud; the court denies him reward, so he rewards his warriors with his own wealth, binding them to his house. The Kanezawa stockade has never been identified by excavation. The city of Yokote treats the hill of the later Kanazawa castle, now Kanazawa Park, as its traditional site, and the marker is placed there. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: A palace succession quarrel is settled not by courtiers but by warriors, the moment the samurai step to the centre of national politics.

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Kiyomori destroys his Minamoto rival and seizes supremacy over the court, the first samurai to dominate Japan, and the spark, twenty years on, of the Genpei War.

names.toponym: Seta Bridge, Ōmi Province (modern Ōtsu, Shiga)

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The largest civil war of ancient Japan: a disputed succession that pitted the late emperor's brother against his son, and remade the imperial state. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: The Itabitsu River, on the Buzen–Chikuzen border (modern Kitakyūshū); Hirotsugu had raised his army at Dazaifu

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: A Nara-period courtier, demoted to a post in Kyushu, raises a revolt against the government, and so unnerves the emperor that he flees the capital and turns to the buddhas for protection, ordering great Kannon images cast and sutras read in every province. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Isawa, Mutsu Province, the Kitakami valley (modern Iwate)

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The long war to conquer the Emishi of the north, and the origin of the title 'Seii Taishōgun,' the barbarian-subduing great general that the shōguns would one day bear. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The Soga clan crushes the Mononobe, settling, by the sword, whether Japan would embrace Buddhism.

names.toponym: Shimo-Akasaka Castle (Lower Akasaka), Kawachi Province (modern Chihayaakasaka, Osaka)

descriptions.value: Kusunoki Masashige's tiny garrison defies the Kamakura shogunate at Akasaka, one of the opening battles of the Genkō War and the birth of a legend of loyalty. A designated national historic site (1934), separately from the upper fort besieged in 1333.

names.toponym: Kami-Akasaka Castle (Upper Akasaka, also called Kusunoki Castle), Kawachi Province (modern Chihayaakasaka, Osaka)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 上赤坂城の戦い (Siege of Kami-Akasaka)
Japanese Wikipedia: 上赤坂城 (Kami-Akasaka Castle)

descriptions.value: The second Akasaka siege. Kusunoki Masashige's new upper fort, held by the noted warrior Hirano Shōgen and Masashige's brother, fell after nine days, but at a cost to the shogunate that a surviving contemporary record lets historians count. A designated national historic site (1934), under the name Kusunoki Castle (Kami-Akasaka).

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Nitta Yoshisada smashes the Hōjō field army on the Musashi plain, opening the road to Kamakura and the shogunate's fall.

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Minamoto no Yoritomo led a vast army north to crush the Northern Fujiwara of Hiraizumi after they killed the fugitive Minamoto no Yoshitsune. The fall of Hiraizumi ended the independent power of the Tōhoku and left Yoritomo master of all Japan, on the eve of his shogunate.

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: A revolt by Wada Yoshimori, head of the shogunate's Board of Retainers (samurai-dokoro), against the dominance of the Hōjō regent Yoshitoki, after Wada kinsmen were arrested for conspiracy. In fierce street fighting across Kamakura the Wada were defeated and annihilated.

Emperor Go-Daigo raised the standard of revolt against the Kamakura shogunate from the fortified mountaintop temple of Kasagi. A shogunate army stormed it by a daring night climb and set it ablaze; Go-Daigo was captured and exiled, yet his rising had opened the Genkō War.

An early Genpei-War clash in which Minamoto no Yukiie attempted a night crossing of the Sunomata River against the Taira and was repulsed. The defeat checked the Minamoto advance toward the capital from the east for a time.

Kiso Yoshinaka, his position in Kyoto crumbling, attacked the Hōjūji palace of the retired Emperor Go-Shirakawa and the courtiers and warrior-monks defending it. His victory made him briefly master of the capital, and prompted Yoritomo to send an army that destroyed him weeks later.

Yoritomo's brothers Yoshitsune and Noriyori forced the Uji river crossing against Kiso Yoshinaka, who had seized the capital. Yoshinaka's army collapsed and he fled, to be hunted down and killed at Awazu, clearing the way for the Minamoto to turn on the Taira.

names.toponym: Kojima, Bizen (Seto Inland Sea coast, modern Okayama)

descriptions.value: A Minamoto victory on the Inland Sea coast as Noriyori's forces pressed the retreating Taira. It was one of the engagements that drove the Taira toward their stronghold at Yashima.

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: A seaborne raid by Jurchen ('Toi') pirates that struck Iki, Tsushima and northern Kyūshū, killing and carrying off many. The Dazaifu government under Fujiwara no Takaie organised the defence and drove the raiders back out to sea, a rare foreign assault on Heian Japan. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

Yamato Japan sent a great fleet to Korea to restore its ally Baekje, and was crushed by the Tang–Silla navy at the mouth of the Geum River. The catastrophe ended Japan's involvement on the peninsula for centuries and spurred a wave of defensive fortifications and reforms at home. Where the river Paekkang (Japanese Hakusukinoe) lay is unsettled. It is argued together with the site of the Paekche fortress of Churyu, and Korean scholars have argued both for the lower Geum (Kŭm) and for the Dongjin (Tongjin) near Buan (Puan), about 30 km apart. The marker copies the encyclopedia's point on the lower Geum, whose round latitude of exactly 36° marks it as a chosen figure.

names.toponym: Ōsumi Province, southern Kyūshū, coordinates approximate

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: A revolt of the Hayato, the indigenous people of southern Kyūshū, against the expanding Nara state. The court sent a large army under Ōtomo no Tabito which, after more than a year of mountain warfare, broke Hayato resistance and brought Ōsumi and Satsuma firmly under imperial control. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Ōmi Province, by Lake Biwa, coordinates approximate

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Also called the Emi Rebellion, this was a failed coup by the once-dominant minister Fujiwara no Nakamaro against the retired Empress Kōken and her favourite, the monk Dōkyō. Nakamaro's forces were cut off and destroyed at Lake Biwa, ending Fujiwara dominance for a generation. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Oshima Peninsula, southern Ezo (Hokkaido), coordinates approximate

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The first major war between the Ainu and the Wajin (Japanese) settlers of southern Ezo, sparked by a trade dispute and the killing of an Ainu man. Led by the chief Koshamain, the Ainu stormed most of the Wajin forts before Takeda Nobuhiro killed Koshamain and broke the rising, the foundation of the later Matsumae domain. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

One of the most famous night attacks of the Sengoku: Hōjō Ujiyasu, badly outnumbered, relieved the besieged Kawagoe Castle with a surprise assault that shattered the great Uesugi coalition. The victory made the Later Hōjō the masters of the Kantō plain.

The 'Viper of Mino', Saitō Dōsan, was overthrown and killed by his son Yoshitatsu at the Nagara River. Dōsan's death, he was Nobunaga's father-in-law and ally, opened the way for Oda Nobunaga's later conquest of Mino.

The future Tokugawa Ieyasu put down the great Ikkō-ikki uprising in his home province of Mikawa, in which many of his own retainers had joined the rebels. His victory ended the threat of the warrior-monk leagues to his power and unified Mikawa behind him.

The first of Oda Nobunaga's three campaigns against the Ikkō-ikki stronghold of Nagashima, set amid the rivers of the Kiso delta. This assault failed bloodily, but Nobunaga returned, and in 1574 annihilated the fortress and its defenders. Three campaigns against the Nagashima league, in 1571, 1573 and 1574, are combined in this entry. Several separate engagements are combined in this entry.

citations.label: English Wikipedia: Siege of Ichijōdani Castle

descriptions.value: Oda Nobunaga overran the Asakura capital of Ichijōdani, ending the clan that had long defied him. The fall of the Asakura, and of the Azai days later, removed two of the chief members of the anti-Nobunaga coalition.

The civil war over the succession to Uesugi Kenshin, who died in 1578 leaving two adopted heirs. Uesugi Kagekatsu defeated his rival Kagetora and secured the Uesugi domain, though the struggle left the clan weakened.

Hideyoshi took Tottori Castle not by storm but by starvation, buying up the region's rice beforehand and blockading the fortress until famine forced its surrender. The commander Kikkawa Tsuneie gave his life to save the garrison.

Hideyoshi besieged Takamatsu by damming a river and flooding the castle into an island. Mid-siege came word that Nobunaga had been killed at the Honnō-ji; Hideyoshi swiftly made peace (the commander Shimizu Muneharu taking his own life) and raced east, the 'Great Return' that led to Yamazaki.

The last stand of the Takeda. As Oda and Tokugawa armies overran Kai, Takeda Katsuyori, abandoned by his vassals, made a final stand and took his own life at Mt Tenmoku, ending the great clan of Shingen.

A revolt by Kunohe Masazane in the far north against Hideyoshi's new order, the final battle of the Sengoku unification. A vast Toyotomi army overwhelmed Kunohe Castle, and with its fall Hideyoshi's authority reached every corner of Japan. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

citations.label: English Wikipedia: Sieges of Gassantoda Castle

descriptions.value: Ōuchi Yoshitaka, with the young Mōri Motonari, marched deep into Izumo to storm the Amago stronghold of Gassantoda, and failed badly. The repulse shattered Ōuchi prestige and helped set Motonari on his own path to power.

An Oda family civil war in which Nobunaga crushed the revolt of his younger brother Nobuyuki and the elders backing him. The victory secured Nobunaga's leadership of the clan at the outset of his rise.

Uesugi Kenshin led a vast Kantō coalition against the Hōjō capital of Odawara, but the fortress held and supply forced him to retreat. It showed both Kenshin's reach and the strength of Odawara's defences, which would defy Shingen too, and only fall to Hideyoshi in 1590.
Takeda Shingen took the Nagano clan's castle of Minowa after a long contest for western Kōzuke. Among its defenders was the famed swordsman Kamiizumi Hidetsuna, founder of the Shinkage-ryū.
Uesugi Kenshin captured the great Noto fortress of Nanao after a long siege and an inside betrayal. With Nanao taken, he turned to meet Oda Nobunaga's relief army and crushed it at Tedorigawa.

Nobunaga's general Araki Murashige rebelled and held out at Arioka (Itami) Castle for over a year. When it fell, Araki escaped but Nobunaga had his abandoned family and hundreds of followers put to death in a notorious reprisal.

Hideyoshi's two-year blockade of Miki Castle, the 'starvation of Miki', broke the Bessho clan's revolt in Harima. Like Tottori after it, it showed Hideyoshi's preference for siege and supply over costly assault.

names.toponym: Arai Castle, Miura Peninsula, Sagami (modern Kanagawa)

descriptions.value: Hōjō Sōun's final blow against the Miura clan, ending a long war for Sagami. The fall of Arai made Sōun, often called the first Sengoku daimyō, master of the province and founded the power of the Later Hōjō.

Takeda Shingen drove into the Kantō and reached the walls of Odawara, but, like Uesugi Kenshin before him, could not crack the Hōjō fortress. He burned the castle town and pulled back, fighting the Hōjō again at Mimasetōge on the retreat.

citations.label: English Wikipedia: Siege of Noda Castle

descriptions.value: Takeda Shingen's last siege. He captured the small Tokugawa fort of Noda, but fell ill or was wounded there and died on the march home, a death that saved the embattled Tokugawa and Oda from his advance on Kyoto.

As the Oda–Tokugawa invasion swept through Takeda lands in 1582, every castle surrendered except Takatō, held by Katsuyori's brother Nishina Morinobu. His defiant last stand and death came just before the Takeda were extinguished at Tenmokuzan.

During Hideyoshi's Odawara campaign, Ishida Mitsunari tried to take Oshi by damming a river and flooding it, but the 'floating castle' withstood the water attack. It gave up only after the main Hōjō capital surrendered, one of the campaign's few defensive successes.

citations.label: English Wikipedia: Siege of Iwaya Castle

descriptions.value: As the Shimazu drove north to conquer Kyūshū, the Ōtomo general Takahashi Jōun made a famous last stand at Iwaya with a tiny garrison against an overwhelming Shimazu army, dying with all his men. The heroic defence bought time before Hideyoshi's intervention saved the Ōtomo.

Chōsokabe Motochika defeated a Toyotomi-allied force under Sengoku Hidehisa at Hiketa in eastern Sanuki, a step in his bid to unify all of Shikoku, a dream Hideyoshi's great invasion would end two years later.

citations.label: English Wikipedia: Battle of Muraki Castle

descriptions.value: One of the young Oda Nobunaga's earliest notable victories: he stormed the Imagawa-held fort of Muraki to relieve his Mizuno allies, reportedly using arquebuses fired in relays, an early sign of the gunnery that would later define his career.

During the third Kawanakajima campaign, Takeda troops under Baba Nobuharu overran the Uesugi-aligned fort of Katsurayama north of Zenkō-ji, wiping out its garrison, one episode in the long Takeda–Uesugi struggle for northern Shinano.

Two linked actions over a Murakami stronghold in Shinano. Takeda Shingen's 1550 assault ended in a bloody repulse remembered as the 'Toishi collapse', one of his worst defeats, before the castle fell in 1551 to the stratagem of Sanada Yukitaka, beginning the Sanada family's rise. Two sieges, the Takeda defeat of 1550 and Sanada Yukitaka's capture of the castle in 1551, are combined in this entry. Several separate engagements are combined in this entry.

citations.label: English Wikipedia: Siege of Yoshida Castle

descriptions.value: Invading Mikawa in 1575, Takeda Katsuyori probed Yoshida Castle, stoutly held for the Tokugawa by Sakai Tadatsugu. Unable to take it, he turned aside to besiege Nagashino instead, the move that led straight to his catastrophe there.

The Shimazu brothers took Takabaru Castle from the Itō, cracking open Itō Yoshisuke's domain in Hyūga and advancing the Shimazu drive to dominate Kyūshū, which soon drove Yoshisuke into the arms of the Ōtomo and on to the great clash at Mimigawa.

names.toponym: Suruga Bay, off Omosu (modern Numazu, Shizuoka)

descriptions.value: A fleet action in Suruga Bay after the Takeda–Hōjō alliance collapsed: the Hōjō navy met the Takeda fleet under Ohama Kagetaka in one of the era's uncommon naval battles. The fighting was indecisive, though the Hōjō claimed the advantage.

Shibata Katsuie's Oda army besieged the Uesugi fortress of Uozu in Etchū through the spring of 1582. The garrison held out and was wiped out almost to a man, the castle falling on the 3rd day of the 6th lunar month (≈22 June 1582), the day after Oda Nobunaga was killed at Honnō-ji, news the defenders never lived to hear.

A struggle within the Oda house itself. The young Nobunaga overcame the rival Kiyosu branch of his own clan, took their castle, and made it his headquarters, a decisive step toward unifying his home province of Owari. A struggle of several years inside the Oda house, ending with the capture of Kiyosu Castle. Several separate engagements are combined in this entry.

citations.label: English Wikipedia: Battle of Fukuda Bay

descriptions.value: The first recorded armed clash between Japanese forces and a European power. The Matsura attacked Portuguese trading carracks anchored at Fukuda Bay near Nagasaki, but the Europeans' shipboard cannon drove the attackers off.

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 稲葉山城の戦い

descriptions.value: Nobunaga's capture of the great mountain fortress of Inabayama broke the Saitō and gave him the province of Mino. He renamed the castle Gifu and took up the seal 'Tenka Fubu', 'the realm under one sword', announcing his ambition to unify Japan.

Takeda Katsuyori captured the formidable Tōtōmi fortress of Takatenjin, a prize his celebrated father, Shingen, had failed to take. It was the high-water mark of Katsuyori's fortunes; overconfidence after it would carry him to disaster at Nagashino the following year.

Tokugawa Ieyasu retook Takatenjin after a long, grinding blockade. Katsuyori dared not march to relieve it, and the abandoned garrison was wiped out, a humiliation that shattered the Takeda's standing and foreshadowed the clan's destruction the next year.

With the Shimazu of Satsuma on the verge of conquering all Kyūshū, Hideyoshi answered the Ōtomo's plea for help and poured a vast army onto the island. Overwhelmed by numbers, the Shimazu submitted, and the whole of Kyūshū passed under Toyotomi authority. A campaign across the whole island. The marker is simply the island's centre, where no fighting took place; the shaded area is the nine provinces of Kyūshū. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it. Area: the nine provinces of Kyūshū (whole units, an approximation).

names.toponym: Takatō Castle, Ina valley, Shinano (modern Ina, Nagano)

descriptions.value: In 1545 Takeda Shingen besieged and captured Takatō Castle in the Ina valley of Shinano, defeating Takatō Yoritsugu and pressing forward the Takeda conquest of the province.

In 1549 (Tenbun 18) Shimazu Takahisa stormed and captured Kajiki castle in Ōsumi, a Shimazu victory remembered as the first battlefield use of Portuguese-derived arquebuses in Japan, the moment European firearms entered the country's wars.

In 1558 (Eiroku 1) the young Matsudaira Motoyasu, the future Tokugawa Ieyasu, led an Imagawa army against Terabe Castle in Mikawa, whose lord had defected to Oda Nobunaga. The assault was driven off by Oda reinforcements, and the action is remembered as Motoyasu's first battle.

In 1563 (Eiroku 6) the allied forces of Hōjō Ujiyasu and Takeda Shingen besieged Matsuyama Castle in Musashi; their 24,000 troops, aided by miners tunnelling beneath the walls, forced the surrender of the 10,000-strong Uesugi and Ōta garrison, tightening the allies' grip on the contested Kantō plain.

In 1570 the Rokkaku besieged Chōkō-ji Castle in Ōmi, which Oda Nobunaga had taken from them two years earlier, and cut off its water. The Oda garrison under Shibata Katsuie sallied out and routed the attackers, lifting the siege.
In 1585 (Tenshō 13) Toyotomi Hideyoshi marched on Toyama Castle in Etchū and overwhelmed the defending Sassa Narimasa, shattering his resistance and securing Toyotomi mastery of the province.

names.toponym: Ueda Castle, Shinano Province (modern Ueda, Nagano)

descriptions.value: In 1600 a Sanada garrison of roughly 2,000 under Sanada Masayuki held Ueda Castle in Shinano against Tokugawa Hidetada's army of some 38,000, and the delay this imposed kept Hidetada from reaching the decisive Battle of Sekigahara in time.

names.toponym: Hasedō Castle, near Yamagata (modern Yamagata Pref.)

descriptions.value: On the northern front of the Sekigahara campaign, the Tokugawa-aligned Mogami Yoshiaki, reinforced by the Date, withstood a far larger Uesugi assault on Hasedō Castle near Yamagata, repelling Naoe Kanetsugu and securing the Tōhoku theatre.

names.toponym: Tanabe Castle, Tango Province (modern Maizuru, Kyoto)

descriptions.value: Some 500 defenders under the poet-general Hosokawa Yūsai held Tanabe Castle in Tango against roughly 15,000 Western Army besiegers; the siege ended inconclusively but tied down a large force that never reached the decisive battle at Sekigahara.

names.toponym: Uto Castle, Higo Province, Kyūshū (modern Kumamoto)

descriptions.value: During the Sekigahara campaign, the Eastern general Katō Kiyomasa besieged Uto Castle in Higo, held for the Western Army by Konishi Yukikage; when word came of the Western defeat, Yukikage surrendered and took his own life, and Kiyomasa absorbed the Konishi lands of Higo.

names.toponym: Yanagawa Castle, Chikugo Province, Kyūshū (modern Fukuoka)

descriptions.value: In the aftermath of Sekigahara, a Tokugawa-aligned army besieged Yanagawa Castle in Chikugo on Kyūshū and forced the surrender of its renowned defender Tachibana Muneshige, a sign that Ieyasu's victory was being enforced even on the far edges of the realm.

names.toponym: South of Osaka Castle, Settsu Province (modern Osaka)

descriptions.value: South of Osaka Castle in 1615, the Tokugawa shogunate crushed the Toyotomi in the final clash of the Summer Campaign, Sanada Yukimura fell, Osaka Castle was taken, and the Toyotomi line was extinguished. It is often called the last great battle between two samurai armies.

At Dōmyōji in 1615, a Tokugawa army defeated the Toyotomi in one of the major clashes of the Osaka Summer Campaign; the celebrated Toyotomi commander Gotō Mototsugu was shot down and committed suicide, one of the battles that led to the fall of Osaka.

names.toponym: Utsunomiya Castle, Shimotsuke Province (modern Utsunomiya, Tochigi)

descriptions.value: In spring 1868 the new Meiji government's imperial army recaptured Utsunomiya Castle from Tokugawa shogunate remnants under Ōtori Keisuke and Hijikata Toshizō, securing an early foothold for the imperial advance north during the Boshin War.

names.toponym: Kamakura (Hokke-dō / Nishi Mikado), Sagami Province (modern Kanagawa)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: Hōji War (宝治合戦)
Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: In 1247 the Hōjō, allied with the Adachi, destroyed the rival Miura clan at Kamakura, driving Miura Yasumura and some five hundred of his kin to mass suicide and cementing Hōjō supremacy over the Kamakura shogunate.

names.toponym: Kamakura, Sagami Province (campaign from Shinano via Musashi; modern Kanagawa)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: Nakasendai Rebellion (中先代の乱)
Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: In 1335 Hōjō Tokiyuki, son of the last Hōjō regent, briefly seized Kamakura and drove out Ashikaga Tadayoshi, but Ashikaga Takauji put down the revolt and took the city for himself; Takauji's move to reward his followers without imperial sanction broke his ties with Emperor Go-Daigo and set Japan on the road to the Ashikaga shogunate. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Kazusa provincial headquarters, Ichihara, Chiba Prefecture

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 平忠常の乱 (Taira no Tadatsune Rebellion)
Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Taira no Tadatsune, the greatest landholder on the Bōsō peninsula, burned out a provincial governor and seized the Kazusa government office, then held off the court for three years. He gave in only when Minamoto no Yorinobu, his former lord, took command, and that surrender handed the Minamoto the east. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Tōmyōji causeway, Fujishima, Echizen Province (modern Nittazuka, Fukui City)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 藤島の戦い (Battle of Fujishima)
Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The death of Nitta Yoshisada, the general who had destroyed Kamakura in 1333. Riding out with about fifty horsemen, he was cornered by a far larger Ashikaga force in the flooded rice country north of Fukui, hit by an arrow and killed himself.

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: The largest Ainu rising against Japanese rule. Shakushain, chief of Shibuchari, united Ainu groups across Ezo against the Matsumae domain's trade monopoly in the summer of 1669, then was murdered at a peace banquet four months later, and the revolt died with him. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia, 大塩平八郎の乱 (Ōshio Heihachirō's Rebellion)
Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: A serving shogunal police officer turned Confucian teacher led some 300 followers against the magistrates of Osaka during the Tenpō famine. The rising was crushed in half a day, but the fires it started burned roughly a fifth of the city.

when.label: June to September 1868 (Keiō 4, fifth to eighth lunar months)

names.toponym: Nagaoka Castle, Echigo Province (modern Nagaoka, Niigata Prefecture)

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Nagaoka domain tried to stay out of the Boshin War, and when the imperial commanders refused to hear it, its chief retainer Kawai Tsugunosuke fought them with modern rifles and two of the only three Gatling guns in Japan. His castle fell, was recaptured in a night crossing of a marsh, then fell for good. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Miyako Bay, Mutsu Province (modern Iwate Prefecture)

descriptions.value: The Ezo Republic's one attempt to go on the offensive: a boarding raid meant to capture the imperial ironclad Kōtetsu at anchor in Miyako Bay. Only one of the three attacking ships arrived, and a Gatling gun cut the boarders down as they dropped onto the ironclad's deck.

names.toponym: Koga Castle, Shimōsa Province (modern Koga, Ibaraki)

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: A twenty eight year civil war for the Kantō, begun when the Kamakura kubō Ashikaga Shigeuji murdered his own deputy, the Kantō kanrei Uesugi Noritada. It split the region along the Tone, created the rival Koga and Horigoe kubō, and for many historians opens the warring states age in the east. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Kami-Koma, Sōraku district, southern Yamashiro Province (modern Kizugawa, Kyoto); one of the league's assembly villages

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: On the eleventh day of the twelfth month of Bunmei 17, a date that falls in January 1486, the warrior landholders of the three southern districts of Yamashiro met in assembly, ordered both warring Hatakeyama armies out of the province, and then governed it themselves for close to eight years. The league governed the three southern districts of Yamashiro, Kuse, Tsuzuki and Sagara, which are shaded. The marker is one point within them. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it. Area: the districts of Kuse, Tsuzuki and Sagara in southern Yamashiro (whole units, an approximation).

properties.title: Invasion of Izu (fall of the Horigoe kubō)

names.toponym: Horigoe palace site, Jike, Izu Province (modern Izunokuni, Shizuoka Prefecture)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 伊豆討ち入り (Invasion of Izu)
Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: In 1493 the shogunal officer Ise Moritoki, later known as Hōjō Sōun, crossed from Suruga into Izu and stormed the palace of the Horigoe kubō, the Ashikaga branch the shogunate had planted there. Its holder fled, the line ended, and Sōun gained the province that became the cradle of the Later Hōjō. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Nagamorihara, Echigo Province (modern Shimobara-shinden, Minamiuonuma, Niigata Prefecture)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 長森原の戦い (Battle of Nagamorihara)

descriptions.value: Retreating from a failed occupation of Echigo, the Kantō kanrei Uesugi Akisada was overtaken on the Nagamorihara plain and died there. Nagao Tamekage, the deputy governor whose revolt had killed Akisada's brother, then held Echigo outright and founded the line that produced Uesugi Kenshin.

Amago Haruhisa brought a reported 30,000 men into Aki to destroy Mōri Motonari, who held Yoshida-Kōriyama with about 3,000. Motonari raided out of the castle all winter until an Ōuchi relief army arrived and drove the Amago off. Aki stayed Ōuchi, and the Mōri became a power in their own right.

when.label: Sixth month, Tenbun 11 to ninth month, Tenbun 17 (1542 to 1548)

names.toponym: Koori Nishiyama Castle, Date district, Mutsu Province (modern Koori, Fukushima)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 天文の乱 (Tenbun no Ran)
Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: A six year civil war inside the Date house, fought between Date Tanemune and his son Harumune over a plan to place a Date son over the Uesugi of Echigo. It pulled in almost every clan of southern Ōu and broke Date power for a generation. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

names.toponym: Eguchi Castle, Settsu Province (modern Higashiyodogawa Ward, Osaka)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: Battle of Eguchi (江口の戦い)

descriptions.value: Miyoshi Nagayoshi trapped his kinsman and rival Miyoshi Masanaga between the Yodo and Kanzaki rivers north of Osaka and destroyed him, breaking the shogunal deputy Hosokawa Harumoto and driving the shogun himself out of Kyoto.

properties.title: Battle of Satta Pass and the Fall of Sunpu

names.toponym: Satta Pass, Suruga Province (modern Shimizu ward, Shizuoka city)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 薩埵峠の戦い (戦国時代) (Battle of Satta Pass, Sengoku period)
Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Takeda Shingen tore up the Kai-Sagami-Suruga alliance and marched on Suruga. His agents had already bought the Imagawa high command, so the defence of Satta Pass dissolved without a real battle and Sunpu fell in a single day.

when.label: Genki 1/9/12 to Tenshō 8/8/2 (11 October 1570 to 10 September 1580)

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Ten years of siege for the fortified temple-city at Osaka, the longest war Nobunaga ever fought. The abbot Kennyo called out the Ikkō-ikki of every province against him, and only when the Mōri supply route was cut at sea did the temple give in and burn. A ten-year war, 1570 to 1580, of many separate engagements around the fortified temple. Several separate engagements are combined in this entry.

names.toponym: Imayama, Hizen Province (modern Kuruma, Yamato-chō, Saga City, Saga)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 今山の戦い (Battle of Imayama)

descriptions.value: Besieged in Saga castle by a far larger Ōtomo army, the Ryūzōji sent about five hundred men out by night against the enemy forward camp on Imayama, killed its commander and wrecked it. The raid made Nabeshima Naoshige's name and set the Ryūzōji on the road to becoming a great Kyūshū power.

names.toponym: Kanegasaki Castle, Tsuruga, Echizen Province (modern Fukui)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: Kanegasaki no nokiguchi (金ヶ崎の戦い)

descriptions.value: Nobunaga had taken Kanegasaki and was pushing into Echizen when his brother-in-law Azai Nagamasa changed sides and closed the road home. He ran for Kyoto with a rearguard holding the pass behind him, and the escape became the most famous fighting withdrawal in Japanese military history.

names.toponym: Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei, above Sakamoto, Ōmi Province (modern Ōtsu, Shiga)

descriptions.value: Nobunaga encircled Mount Hiei and burned Enryaku-ji, the head temple of the Tendai school, together with the town of Sakamoto below it. Six centuries of monastic military power ended in a day. The standard teaching case for his campaign against Japan's armed temples. The temple complex of Enryaku-ji, rebuilt after the burning, stands on its original ground.

names.toponym: Odani Castle, Ōmi Province (modern Nagahama, Shiga)

descriptions.value: Nobunaga's final reckoning with the brother-in-law who had betrayed him. With the Asakura destroyed days earlier, the Azai stronghold on Mount Odani was split in two and stormed. The clan was wiped out, and Hideyoshi received northern Ōmi as the first domain he held in his own name.

properties.title: Nobunaga's Suppression of the Echizen Ikkō-ikki

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 越前一向一揆 (Echizen Ikkō-ikki)
Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: Echizen threw off Oda rule in 1574 and became a province governed by the Honganji and its congregations. In 1575 Nobunaga returned with some thirty thousand men, broke the ikki within days, and handed the province to Shibata Katsuie, whose castle at Kitanoshō became the Oda base in the north. A campaign across the province of Echizen, which is shaded. The marker is Fuchū, the provincial capital. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it. Area: the province of Echizen (whole units, an approximation).

names.toponym: Oyama Gobō, Kaga Province (site of Kanazawa Castle, Kanazawa, Ishikawa)

descriptions.value: The fortified cathedral that served as the capital of Ikkō-ikki Kaga fell to Shibata Katsuie and Sakuma Morimasa. Ninety-two years of rule by a Buddhist league ended, and Morimasa raised a castle on the ridge; three years later it became the Maeda seat of Kanazawa.

names.toponym: Wakamiko Castle, Kai Province (modern Hokuto, Yamanashi)

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: When Oda Nobunaga was killed in 1582, the former Takeda provinces of Kai and Shinano were left with no ruler, and the Tokugawa, the Later Hōjō and the Uesugi all marched in to claim them. Tokugawa Ieyasu, badly outnumbered, held on for eighty days and came away with two new provinces. Fought over Kai, Shinano and Kōzuke, which are shaded, after Oda rule there collapsed. The marker is Wakamiko, the Hōjō camp facing the Tokugawa. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it. Area: Kai, Shinano and Kōzuke (whole units, an approximation).

when.label: Tenshō 13, 6th to 8th months (12 July to 30 August 1585)

citations.label: Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: In the summer of 1585 Hideyoshi sent about a hundred thousand men across the Inland Sea in three columns to break Chōsokabe Motochika, who had just made himself master of all four provinces of Shikoku. Within two months Motochika submitted, keeping only his native Tosa. Hideyoshi's armies invaded Shikoku through Awa, Sanuki and Iyo, which are shaded. The marker is Ichinomiya Castle in Awa, one of the sieges. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it. Area: Awa, Sanuki and Iyo (whole units, an approximation).

names.toponym: Jōmura Castle, Yamaga, Higo Province (modern Kumamoto Prefecture)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 肥後国人一揆 (Higo kokujin ikki)
Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: When Sassa Narimasa forced a cadastral survey on the warrior houses of Higo, the whole province rose against him. The revolt held him off for five months, cost him his life, and left Higo to be carved up between Katō Kiyomasa and Konishi Yukinaga. Its scale helped prompt Hideyoshi's sword hunt of 1588. A rising of the local lords across the province of Higo, which is shaded. The marker is Jōmura Castle. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it. Area: the province of Higo (whole units, an approximation).

names.toponym: Jūgorigahara, Tomoe, Tagawa District, Dewa Province (modern Tsuruoka, Yamagata Pref.)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 十五里ヶ原の戦い (Battle of Jūgorigahara)

descriptions.value: While Mogami Yoshiaki was pinned down against Date Masamune in the Ōsaki war, Honjō Shigenaga led an Uesugi army into Shōnai and destroyed the Mogami force under the Tōzenji brothers on the plain west of Tsuruoka, winning the Shōnai rice plain and the port of Sakata for Uesugi Kagekatsu.

names.toponym: Teraike Castle, Mutsu (modern Toyoma, Tome, Miyagi)

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: Kasai-Ōsaki ikki (葛西大崎一揆)
Placed by hand by the atlas author; no published source coordinate identified

descriptions.value: When Hideyoshi's Ōshū settlement dispossessed the Kasai and Ōsaki and handed their thirteen districts to an outsider, the whole country rose. The new lord was besieged in his own fief, and the man sent to rescue him, Date Masamune, was widely believed to have started it. The entry stands for a war or campaign over a wider area; the point is one place associated with it.

Odawara was fortified from the Kamakura period and passed in 1495 to Ise Moritoki, founder of the Odawara Hōjō. Five generations of the Hōjō turned it into the administrative centre of a domain covering most of the Kantō, with water moats on the low side, dry ditches on the hill side, banks and cliffs that turned back Uesugi Kenshin in 1561 and Takeda Shingen in 1569. Toyotomi Hideyoshi broke it in 1590 with a three month siege and bluff rather than an assault, then ordered most of the works razed. The Edo period castle rebuilt by Ōkubo Tadayo fitted entirely inside what had been the third bailey of the Hōjō fortress; its keep was pulled down between 1870 and 1872, and the present concrete keep dates from 1960.

Edo Castle was begun in 1457 by Ōta Dōkan in Toshima District of Musashi Province and was taken by Hōjō Ujitsuna in 1524. Tokugawa Ieyasu made it his seat after 1590 and, from 1603, the headquarters of the shogunate, which it remained until 1867. Its outermost moat enclosed ground now occupied by Tokyo Station, the Marunouchi district and Kitanomaru Park, an area far larger than the present palace grounds. After the Meiji Restoration the site became the Tokyo Imperial Palace, and moats, ramparts and stretches of wall survive.

Kawagoe stood at the centre of the fifteenth and sixteenth century contest for the Kantō between the Late Hōjō and the two branches of the Uesugi. Hōjō Ujitsuna seized it in 1537, thirteen years after taking Edo, and it became a forward base commanding the road to Echigo and the line of the Arakawa. The Uesugi attempt to recover it ended in the celebrated night battle at Kawagoe, after which Uesugi power in the region collapsed and Kawagoe served for some forty five years as a satellite fortress screening Edo and Odawara. It was the seat of Kawagoe Domain throughout the Edo period; dismantling began in 1870, leaving the Honmaru Goten and a yagura mound on the original site.

Hachigata was built about 1476 by Nagao Kageharu on a spur enclosed by the Arakawa and Fukasawa rivers, and its position at the western edge of the Kantō plain made it a key to Musashi Province. Hōjō Ujikuni took charge of the northern Hōjō holdings in 1564 and rebuilt it with wide dry moats and clay ramparts at the foot of the hill, using stone facing at the main gate as a display of authority; the defences eventually ran nearly a kilometre along the ridge. Takeda Shingen failed to take it in 1568. In 1590 Ujikuni held out for a month with roughly 3,000 men against some 30,000 under Maeda Toshiie and Uesugi Kagekatsu before surrendering on terms that spared his garrison, after which the castle was demolished.

Hōjō Ujiteru began Hachiōji Castle on Mount Fukasawa in the 1570s, after Takeda troops nearly overran his earlier seat at Takiyama in 1569, and he moved his household there by 1587. It guarded the Kobotoke and Ange passes on the road between Kai and Musashi, with a stone lined approach and a drawbridge before the main gate, yet the hilltop inner bailey was small and barely defended, evidence that the work was never finished. In 1590 Ujiteru was away at Odawara and left about 1,300 defenders; the Toyotomi detachment under Maeda Toshiie and Uesugi Kagekatsu attacked at dawn on 23 June and took the castle within the day. Tokugawa Ieyasu ordered the site destroyed and it was shunned for years as haunted; the stone walls, moat bridge and residence entrance seen today were reconstructed in 1990.

Kasugayama was a yamashiro spread over two ridges of the 180 metre Mount Kasuga, built without stone walls and relying instead on terraced enclosures with earthen ramparts and dry moats. Probably raised by Nagao Tamekage, it passed in 1548 to Uesugi Kenshin and served as his base for the Kawanakajima campaigns against Takeda Shingen. Uesugi Kagekatsu secured it after the succession struggle that followed Kenshin's death in 1578, and when the Uesugi were transferred to Aizu in 1598 the castle went to Hori Hideharu, who moved his seat to Fukushima Castle near the port of Naoetsu in 1600. Kasugayama was deserted by 1607 and has been a National Historic Site since 1935.

Strategic castle on a plateau controlling the Mikuni route between Kozuke and Echigo; the disputed Numata territory between the Sanada and Hojo was a direct trigger of Hideyoshi's 1590 Odawara campaign. Japanese sources class it as a hill castle (okajiro).

Stronghold of the Nagano clan under the renowned Nagano Narimasa, who long resisted Takeda Shingen's invasions of western Kozuke; finally fell to Shingen in 1566 and later passed to Ii Naomasa. One of the Top 100 Castles of Japan.

Formidable mountain castle of the Sano clan in southern Shimotsuke; famed for reputedly repelling repeated attacks by Uesugi Kenshin, it sat at the contested frontier between the Uesugi, Hojo, and Satake spheres.

Long-held seat of the powerful Utsunomiya clan, who governed central Shimotsuke from the late Heian era (c. 1063) for roughly five centuries; a key player in the Kanto power struggles before being dispossessed by Hideyoshi in 1597.

citations.label: Japanese Wikipedia: 小山城 (下野国)

descriptions.value: Flatland castle of the Oyama clan, shugo of Shimotsuke; in 1380 it was the focus of the Oyama Yoshimasa Rebellion against the Kamakura kubo, a major Nanboku-cho/early-Muromachi conflict in the Kanto.

Center of the Aizu basin, seat of the Ashina clan and briefly of Date Masamune after his 1589 victory at Suriagehara; rebuilt as a major modern castle by Gamo Ujisato. Later famous for the 1868 Boshin War siege.

Yonezawa was a flatland castle in southern Dewa held first by the Nagai and then by the Date, and Date Masamune was born here in 1567. Uesugi Kagekatsu received it in 1597, and after Sekigahara cut the clan from 1,200,000 to 300,000 koku the Uesugi rebuilt it between 1608 and 1613, leaving the earthen ramparts unfaced with stone and the keep at a modest three storeys so as not to attract Tokugawa suspicion. They also moved the grave of their founder Uesugi Kenshin from Echigo to within the walls. Clan revenues were halved again in 1664, all remaining buildings were pulled down in 1873, and Uesugi Shrine now stands on the site of the keep.

Yamagata Castle guarded the southern end of the Yamagata Basin, where the Ushu Kaido met the routes to Shonai and to Sendai, and it was the seat of the Mogami clan for roughly 275 years. Mogami Yoshiaki rebuilt it in 1592 with second and third baileys and a ring of two and three storey yagura, but no tenshu was ever raised on its prepared foundation. After Yoshiaki backed Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1600 the Mogami were raised to 570,000 koku, only to be attainted in 1622, after which a rapid succession of poorer daimyo let the main bailey fall into ruin and part of the outer bailey be ploughed up. The site is now Kajo Park, where the second bailey's Higashi Otemon was rebuilt in 1991 as part of a restoration programme running to 2033.

Hatakeyama Takakuni established a fortified residence here in 1341 on a spur of the Adatara mountains commanding the Oshu Kaido, and his line took the Nihonmatsu name. In 1585 Nihonmatsu Yoshitsugu seized Date Terumune as a hostage and both men died in the Date counterattack; Date Masamune burned and then rebuilt the castle in 1587 as a border fortress against the Ashina. From 1643 the Niwa clan abandoned the hilltop enclosure and rebuilt the castle at the foot of the hill, ruling Nihonmatsu Domain from there until the Meiji Restoration. In the Boshin War of 1868 it fell in a single day to superior Sattcho firepower, with 337 Nihonmatsu samurai killed, and the surviving structures were demolished in 1872.

Satake Yoshinobu began Kubota Castle in 1603, after Tokugawa Ieyasu transferred the clan from its Hitachi homeland to northern Dewa, completing the main bailey in 1604 and laying out a castle town that was extended repeatedly through the 1620s and 1630s. Built on a low hill above the Nibetsu River, it relied on wet moats, earthworks and eight yagura rather than stone walls, and it never had an imposing keep, possibly to avoid attracting shogunal suspicion. Fires in 1633, 1776, 1778 and 1797 repeatedly gutted it, and after the Satake surrendered the castle in 1869 a final fire in 1880 destroyed the abandoned main bailey. The grounds became Senshu Park, where a corner yagura was reconstructed in 1989 and the front gate in 2001.

Oda Nobunaga had Azuchi built between 1576 and 1579 on Mount Azuchi above Lake Biwa, with Niwa Nagahide supervising, close enough to watch the approaches to Kyoto but clear of the capital's fires and disorder. Its keep rose seven levels, six above ground and one below, with an octagonal top storey, a facade painted with tigers and dragons and interiors by Kano Eitoku, making it as much a political display as a fortress. Nobunaga chartered a tax-free castle town below it in 1577 that held roughly 5,000 people by 1582, and staged the Azuchi religious debate there in 1579. The castle burned within weeks of his death at Honno-ji in 1582 and was never rebuilt; the stone foundations and stairways on the hill are a Special National Historic Site.

The hill fort begun by the Nikaido in the early thirteenth century grew into Inabayama Castle, stronghold of Saito Dosan, the so-called Viper of Mino, and of his descendants. Oda Nobunaga besieged and took it in 1567, renamed both castle and town Gifu after a Chinese precedent, rebuilt it on a grander scale with a mountaintop tenshu, and used it as his main base for about ten years before moving to Azuchi and handing Gifu to his son Oda Nobutada. It fell again after a single day's fighting in 1600, in the prelude to Sekigahara, and in 1603 Okudaira Nobumasa abandoned it for the new Kano Castle at the foot of the mountain, re-erecting some of its structures there. The present keep on Mount Kinka is a 1950s concrete and steel reconstruction that replaced a 1910s wooden one destroyed by fire in 1943.
Nobunaga's main Owari base from 1555; site of the 1582 Kiyosu Conference where the Oda succession was decided after Honnō-ji.
Bluff castle commanding the Kiso River on the Owari–Mino border; its keep is one of Japan's twelve surviving original tenshu and a National Treasure.
Birthplace of Tokugawa Ieyasu (1543) and the ancestral seat of the Matsudaira clan; cradle of the Mikawa power base that grew into the Tokugawa shogunate.
Ieyasu's stronghold in Tōtōmi for ~17 years; he marched from here to the disastrous 1572 Battle of Mikatagahara against Takeda Shingen. Later called the 'castle of success.'
Heart of the Imagawa domain where the young Ieyasu was held hostage; he retired here as Ōgosho, ruling Japan from behind the scenes until his death in 1616. Coordinates approx (plain flatland site).

Fortified residence of the Takeda for three generations (Nobutora, Shingen, Katsuyori); the administrative center of Kai, reflecting Shingen's maxim that men, not walls, are the castle. Now Takeda Shrine.
Originally Fukashi Castle, contested by Ogasawara and Takeda in Shinano; its black-clad keep (built 1590s) is Japan's oldest surviving five-tier tenshu and a National Treasure, ringed by water moats.
Sanada Masayuki's fortress that twice repelled far larger Tokugawa armies (1585 and 1600), delaying Hidetada's force before Sekigahara, a celebrated feat of the Sanada clan.
Mountain seat of the Azai clan in northern Ōmi; fell to Nobunaga's 1573 siege, ending Azai Nagamasa (Nobunaga's brother-in-law) and his ally Asakura. One of Japan's five great mountain castles.
Strategic mountain castle guarding the Ōmi corridor; held by Ishida Mitsunari, leader of the Western Army at Sekigahara (1600). Its functions were later moved to nearby Hikone Castle.
Coastal flatland castle at the mouth of the Ibi/Nagara rivers guarding the Tōkaidō crossing into Ise; major Tokugawa-era fortification developed by Honda Tadakatsu after 1601.
Small river-confluence fortress whose heroic defense by Okudaira Sadamasa triggered the 1575 Battle of Nagashino, where Oda–Tokugawa massed gunfire shattered the Takeda cavalry.

descriptions.value: Mountain fortress above the Asakura clan's castle town in Echizen, a flourishing cultural capital; Nobunaga destroyed it in 1573, and its excavated townscape is now a Special Historic Site.

Key Takeda hilltop castle in southern Shinano; scene of the fierce 1582 last stand of Nishina Morinobu against Oda Nobutada during the Oda conquest of the Takeda. Famous today for its cherry blossoms.
Toyotomi Hideyoshi's grand headquarters from 1583 and seat of his regime; site of the 1614-1615 Sieges of Osaka that ended the Toyotomi house and sealed Tokugawa supremacy.
Tokugawa Ieyasu's Kyoto residence and symbol of shogunal authority near the imperial court; in 1867 Tokugawa Yoshinobu announced the return of power to the Emperor here, ending the shogunate.
Japan's finest surviving original castle and a UNESCO World Heritage Site; held in the Sengoku era by the Kuroda and Hashiba, then rebuilt into its iconic white form by Ikeda Terumasa after 1600.
The highest castle in Japan with an original keep (atop 430m Mt. Gagyu); a strategic Bitchu stronghold contested between the Mimura, Mori and Ukita during the Sengoku wars.
