descriptions.value: Site of Hashiba (Toyotomi) Hideyoshi's notorious 1581 starvation siege ('Tottori no kaw-zeme'), one of the cruelest blockades of the Sengoku period. Hilltop fort on Mt. Kyusho.

Impregnable mountain seat of the Amago clan, who dominated the Izumo region; repelled a major Ōuchi siege in 1542-43 (led by Ōuchi Yoshitaka, with Mōri Motonari as an ally) before finally falling to Mori Motonari in 1566.
Sprawling mountain fortress (270+ enclosures) and birthplace of Mori power; Mori Motonari's 1540-41 defence here against a far larger Amago army launched his rise to mastery of western Honshu.
Rare surviving moated low-hill castle on the Dogo plain; for two centuries the seat of the Kono clan who ruled Iyo Province until conquered by the Toyotomi-backed forces in 1585.
Final headquarters of Chosokabe Motochika, unifier of Shikoku, after 1591; overlooks Tosa Bay. The Chosokabe were dispossessed here following their defeat at Sekigahara in 1600.
Massive fortress built by master castle-builder Kato Kiyomasa from 1591, famed for its curved 'musha-gaeshi' stone walls; later withstood the 1877 Satsuma Rebellion siege.

Funai Castle stands on the coast at Ōita, on the site of the medieval provincial centre of Bungo. Construction began in 1597 under Fukuhara Naotaka, a vassal of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and the castle was completed in 1599 as Niage Castle; Takenaka Shigetoshi, installed after Sekigahara, rebuilt it on a larger scale between 1601 and 1607. A great fire in 1743 destroyed most of the buildings including the three storey tenshu, which was never raised again, and the main gate with three turrets burned in the 1945 air raid on Ōita. Two Edo period turrets, the Hitojichi and Sōmon yagura, still stand together with stretches of stone wall, earthen wall and moat.

Kagoshima Castle, known locally as Tsurumaru, was begun by Shimazu Tadatsune after the Battle of Sekigahara and completed in 1604 as the seat of Satsuma. It was deliberately built in yakata style, more a large fortified residence than a fortress, with no tenshu and no high stone walls, a modest design intended as a political statement of Shimazu submission to the Tokugawa; Tadatsune's father Shimazu Yoshihiro objected that it was indefensible and too close to the sea. His misgivings were borne out during the Anglo-Satsuma War of 1863, although the British gunners mistook a nearby Buddhist temple for the castle tower and shelled that instead. The main citadel burned in 1873 and the second citadel during the Satsuma Rebellion of 1877; the site now holds the Reimeikan prefectural history centre, and the Goromon gate was reconstructed in 2020.

Tachibanayama Castle crowned the 367 metre Mount Tachibana north east of Hakata, a sprawling mountain fortress that used the whole massif of seven peaks and was known as the fortress of Chikuzen. It was raised in 1330 by Ōtomo Sadatoshi, second son of the Bungo shugo Ōtomo Sadamune, and his line took the Tachibana name from the place. Commanding the port of Hakata, it was fought over for decades by the Ōtomo, Ōuchi and Mōri, and in 1586 the young Tachibana Muneshige held it against a large Shimazu army that had just taken his birth father's Iwaya Castle. It was abandoned after Kuroda Nagamasa began Fukuoka Castle in 1601, much of its masonry being carried off for the new work, so that only traces of stone wall and an old well survive at the summit.

Saiki Castle was a yamajiro on the 144 metre Mount Yahata (Hachiman-yama), above the delta at the mouth of the Bansho River on the southern border of Bungo. Mōri Takamasa, relocated there by Tokugawa Ieyasu in 1601 with a holding of 20,000 koku, built it between 1602 and 1606 and laid out a new castle town below, replacing the remote Togamure Castle of the old Saeki clan. The design was overseen by Ichida Yusada, formerly involved in the building of Azuchi, and the stone walls by a master who had worked on those of Himeji; the three storey tenshu was lost to fire only about fifteen years after completion. Because the mountain site was inconvenient in peacetime, a sannomaru was built at the foot of the hill in 1637 for the daimyō residence and domain offices, and the Mōri ruled Saiki for twelve generations until the buildings were sold off or destroyed in 1871.

Oka Castle ran for over a kilometre along the ridge of Tenjinyama above Taketa in south western Bungo, flanked by the Inaba and Tamaki rivers and commanding the roads that cross central Kyushu. Legend dates its origin to 1185 and Shiga Sadatomo is said to have enlarged and renamed it in 1334, though the early record is uncertain. Its most celebrated moment came in 1586, when Shiga Chikatsugu and some 2,000 men held the castle against a Shimazu army numbering over 30,000 until Toyotomi Hideyoshi intervened; from 1594 the Nakagawa clan held it for thirteen generations without transfer or reduction. The tenshu collapsed in an earthquake in 1769, fire destroyed much of the rest in 1771, and the surviving structures were demolished by 1873, leaving the towering stone ramparts that inspired Taki Rentarō's Kōjō no Tsuki.

Kanegasaki sits on a wooded ridge about 86 metres high that drops straight into Tsuruga Bay, guarding the harbour where the routes north from Lake Biwa reach the Japan Sea. A fort was first raised here by Taira no Michimori during the Genpei War of the 1180s, against Kiso Yoshinaka; the ridge was refortified by later lords of Echizen and in the Sengoku period belonged to the Asakura.

Two famous episodes belong to it. In 1337 Nitta Yoshisada held Kanegasaki for the Southern Court, sheltering two sons of Emperor Go-Daigo. Ashikaga forces besieged it for three months; Yoshisada slipped away to Somayama to raise a relief force, but the counter-attack failed and the garrison was reduced to eating its horses. When Kō no Moroyasu broke through in the spring of 1337, Prince Takanaga and Yoshisada's son Nitta Yoshiaki took their own lives along with some three hundred followers. Prince Tsunenaga escaped, only to be caught and killed. It was the end of Nitta resistance in the Hokuriku.

In 1570 Oda Nobunaga invaded Echizen to punish Asakura Yoshikage, stormed the neighbouring hill of Tezutsuyama and took Kanegasaki the next day, the assault led by Kinoshita Tōkichirō, the future Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Word then came that Nobunaga's brother-in-law Azai Nagamasa had changed sides and was closing the road home. Nobunaga bolted for Kyoto while Hideyoshi, with Akechi Mitsuhide, commanded the rearguard that held the pass behind him. The retreat from Kanegasaki became one of the best known feats of Hideyoshi's career, and Nobunaga's revenge followed at Anegawa that summer and at Odani in 1573.

Nothing is built on the hill today. Visitors find terraced enclosures, dry moats cut across the ridge and the footings of the main hall and gate; the site has been a National Historic Site since 1934. At the foot of the slope stands Kanegasaki-gū, a shrine founded in 1890 by the Meiji government to commemorate the princes who died here. The castle was also known as Tsuruga Castle after its town, which is a different place from the Tsuruga Castle of Aizu-Wakamatsu.

Chihaya was thrown up around 1332 by Kusunoki Masashige, a landholder of the Chihaya-Akasaka district of Kawachi, on a ridge running down from Mount Kongō at the Yamato border, roughly five kilometres above his main base at Akasaka. It was a pure mountain fortress with no stone walls and no keep. Five enclosures were strung along about 200 metres of ridge and separated from one another by dry moats, defended by timber palisades, earth banks, removable bridges and cliffs falling away to rivers on both sides. The only approach was a climb of some five hundred steep, narrow steps. The main enclosure measured about 100 by 20 metres and may have carried a single wooden tower, yet the place could hold several hundred men and, decisively, had its own well.

In 1333 the Kamakura shogunate sent a large army against Kusunoki after he emerged from hiding and struck at shogunal positions in Kii, Osaka and Kyoto. The attackers took nearby Kami-Akasaka in a fortnight, then stalled at Chihaya for months. Assaults failed on the slope, the valley was too cramped for proper siege works, and mountain ascetics loyal to Prince Moriyoshi carried supplies in over Mount Kongō. The chronicle Taiheiki credits Kusunoki with constant raids, felled trees and rolled boulders, and straw dummies that drew wasted volleys. The siege tied down shogunal strength and cost it enormous prestige while Emperor Go-Daigo escaped from Oki and Ashikaga Takauji changed sides; Kamakura fell the same year. Chihaya then served as the Kusunoki family seat until 1392, when Hatakeyama Motokuni of the Northern Court defeated Kusunoki Masakatsu and the castle was abandoned.

Nothing built stands today. The ruins have been a National Historic Site since 1934 and the site was named one of Japan's Top 100 Castles in 2006. What survives is the earthwork itself: the terraced enclosures along the ridge, the dry moats cut between them and the long stone stairway. A Meiji period shrine to Masashige, Chihaya Jinja, occupies the second bailey, with its offices in the third.

Nanao sits on a ridge about 300 metres above Nanao Bay at the north end of the Sekidō range, and the name comes from the seven spurs that branch off it. The Hatakeyama began fortifying the ridge early in the fifteenth century, after Hatakeyama Mitsunori was made shugo (military governor) of Noto in 1408, and the family ruled the province from this mountain for roughly 180 years. Hatakeyama Yoshifusa (1491 to 1545) turned a hill fort into one of the five largest mountain castles of medieval Japan, running some 2.5 km north to south and 1 km east to west. The plan was a ladder of terraced baileys: the lord's enclosure stood at the summit and could be reached only by climbing through the walled compounds of the senior retainers, the Yusa and the Chō, with lesser vassals below them and a fortified castle town on the flat ground at the foot. Uesugi Kenshin invaded Noto in 1576, reduced the outlying forts, and could not take the mountain. He returned in 1577 and Nanao held out for about a year, until its lord Hatakeyama Yoshitaka died, of epidemic or of poison depending on the account, leaving a child as nominal head while the chief retainers quarrelled. Yusa Tsugumitsu opened the gates to the Uesugi in the ninth month of 1577, and the Chō, who wanted to fight on, were killed. Kenshin climbed to the summit bailey and wrote to his retainers about the view, then destroyed the Oda relief army under Shibata Katsuie at the Tedori River. Oda forces took Noto in 1581 and Maeda Toshiie received the province; he preferred a site down by the harbour, and Nanao was abandoned in 1589. Because nothing was ever built over it, Nanao is among the best preserved mountain castle sites in Japan. Rough piled stone walls survive around almost every bailey, most strikingly the five stepped tiers at the main enclosure and at the Sakura no baba parade ground. The ruins have been a National Historic Site since 1934, and there is a castle museum at the foot of the climb. The Noto earthquake of 1 January 2024 brought down parts of the walls at the main and second enclosures and at the Sakura no baba.

Miki stood on a terrace above the Mino River, on the road between Kyoto and the Arima hot springs, and Japanese tradition counts it with Gochaku and Aga as one of the three great castles of Harima. It was raised around 1492 by Bessho Noriharu, an Akamatsu deputy rewarded with eight districts after he helped restore his lord to the governorship, and it stayed the seat of his line for some ninety years. His grandson Bessho Nariharu was driven out briefly by the Uragami in 1530, held off two Amago invasions in 1538 and 1539, and bent to the Miyoshi around 1550 before recovering his independence; the castle was much enlarged in those years. Cliffs, valleys and the river closed it on nearly every side, leaving only the south east open to attack.

In 1578 Noriharu's descendant Bessho Nagaharu broke with Oda Nobunaga just as Hashiba Hideyoshi opened the western campaign. Hideyoshi answered with a blockade rather than an assault, ringing Miki with siege forts and earth walls and starving it for roughly twenty months, a campaign remembered as the starving out of Miki. The defeat of the Mōri fleet at Kizugawa in late 1578 and the Ukita defection in 1579 shut the last routes in. Nagaharu surrendered in January 1580 and took his own life on terms that spared his garrison.

Hideyoshi's officers held Miki as a local strongpoint until it was wound up in the mid 1610s under the Tokugawa rule of one castle per province. The main bailey is now Uenomaru Park, with the city history museum beside it, and baileys, earthen banks, dry ditches, wells and the platform of the keep can still be traced, along with a stele carrying Nagaharu's farewell poem. In 2013 the castle site was designated a National Historic Site together with the ring of Hideyoshi's siege forts and ramparts around it.

Takatenjin stood on Mount Kakuo, a steep hill of 132 metres in Totomi rising about 100 metres above the surrounding country, climbable only by narrow paths. Stories of a twelfth century fort are unproven; excavated pottery suggests a stronghold here by the late fifteenth century, and the first firm record is of Kushima Sukeharu holding it for the Imagawa in the early sixteenth. After the Kushima fell in the Hanakura succession war of 1536 the Imagawa passed it to the Ogasawara, who went over to Tokugawa Ieyasu when the Imagawa collapsed. Contemporaries called it the key to Totomi, commanding the roads to the coast and the Tokaido eleven kilometres south.

Takeda Shingen besieged it in 1571 and failed. His son Katsuyori stormed it in 1574, carrying the second bailey and forcing the surrender of Ogasawara Ujisuke, also recorded as Nagatada; taking what his father could not made Katsuyori's name. He then extended the castle west along the ridge, where Takatenjin Shrine now stands, and installed Okabe Motonobu as governor. Ieyasu answered with patience. He seized Suwahara Castle to cut the supply road from the Oi River, built Yokosuka Castle and six siege forts around the mountain, and from 1580 simply starved the garrison out; a letter from Nobunaga instructing him to refuse any surrender survives. Late in the third month of 1581 Okabe led his remaining men out in a hopeless charge and was killed. Katsuyori's failure to relieve the place destroyed his standing with his own vassals, and the Takeda were finished the next year.

Takatenjin was abandoned after 1581 and never refortified, which is why so much of it survives. There is no stone walling. The baileys, earthen ramparts and cut ditches of a late Takeda mountain castle lie almost undisturbed under the trees, together with the ridge path by which the inspector Yokota Tadatoshi escaped to carry news of the fall to Katsuyori. The ruins are a National Historic Site, designated in 1975 and extended in 2007, and number 147 of the Continued Top 100 Castles. A mock keep put up before the Second World War burned after a lightning strike, leaving only its concrete footing; Takatenjin Shrine stands on the summit.

Hosokawa Fujitaka, better known by his Buddhist name Yūsai, built Tanabe in 1582 on the site of an earlier Isshiki fortification, on flat ground hemmed in by the Isatsu and Takano rivers, with Maizuru Bay to the north and marsh to the south. The cramped site forced an unusually compact plan, the baileys wrapped in rings around the centre rather than spread along a ridge. In 1600 Fujitaka held it with about 500 men while his son Tadaoki rode east with Tokugawa Ieyasu, and roughly 15,000 troops of the western coalition closed in. The siege ran some fifty days and was never pressed hard; many of the besiegers had studied poetry under Fujitaka and are said to have fired their cannon without shot. He was by then the last living holder of the Kokin denju, the secret transmission of how to read the tenth century Kokin Wakashū anthology, and rather than let it die with him he sent the certificates out of the castle to Prince Hachijō Toshihito. The court, alarmed that the tradition would be lost, dispatched imperial envoys with a decree ordering the fighting stopped, and Fujitaka gave up the castle nineteen days before Sekigahara, having tied down a substantial western force for the whole campaign. Tanabe then became a domain seat, held by the Kyōgoku from 1621 and the Makino from 1668 until the Meiji Restoration; the domain was renamed Maizuru in 1869 to end the confusion with Tanabe in Kii Province. The buildings were cleared in the 1870s and every moat has since been filled in. The site is now Maizuru Park, where stretches of stone wall, the stone platform of the keep and a garden survive, along with a two storey corner turret rebuilt in 1940 as the Shōkokan and a gate reconstructed in 1992 that houses the castle museum.

Yanagawa stands on the Chikugo delta a few kilometres from the Ariake Sea, on ground so flat that its whole defence was water. Kamachi Haruhisa built it between 1501 and 1504 as an outwork of Kamachi Castle and then moved his house into it; his grandson Kamachi Akimori rebuilt it in earnest in the 1560s, laying out the lattice of channels that made it the hardest place in Kyushu to take. A jingle sung in the Ōtomo camp allowed three months for Higo and a morning for Hizen and Chikuzen, but three years for Yanagawa. Ryūzōji Takanobu and Nabeshima Naoshige could not storm it with twenty thousand men, and neither could the Ōtomo generals Tachibana Dōsetsu and Takahashi Jōun. The Kamachi were destroyed by treachery instead in 1581, and Ryūzōji retainers moved into the castle they had failed to carry. After Hideyoshi's Kyushu campaign of 1587 it went to Dōsetsu's adopted son Tachibana Muneshige at 132,000 koku. Muneshige backed the losing Western army in 1600, was besieged here by Katō Kiyomasa, Kuroda Yoshitaka and Nabeshima Naoshige, and gave the castle up on terms. Tanaka Yoshimasa then held all Chikugo at 325,000 koku and enlarged the works to match; when his line died out without an heir in 1620, Muneshige was brought back at 109,000 koku, the only lord stripped of his domain after Sekigahara who ever recovered it. The Tachibana held Yanagawa until 1871. Fire gutted the castle in February 1872, possibly set to keep the family's treasures from the new government, and the five storey keep, known from a photograph taken about 1870, was never rebuilt; in 1874 its stone was carted away to patch a breached sea dyke. The honmaru, a city historic site, is now school ground, the keep platform left as a grassy hummock the pupils run up for training. What really survives is the water. Some 470 km of canals still thread the town and are worked by flat punts, and Ohana, the Tachibana villa begun west of the castle in 1697, keeps its Shōtō-en garden.

Hikone was begun by Ii Naomasa, one of Tokugawa Ieyasu's most trusted generals, who was granted eastern Omi after Sekigahara (1600) together with Ishida Mitsunari's former seat at Sawayama. Naomasa disliked Sawayama; it was an old-fashioned hill fort split awkwardly between summit and slope, and it carried the taint of the defeated enemy. He chose instead a low hill, Mount Konki, then standing directly on the shore of Lake Biwa, where the Nakasendo highway squeezed through a natural bottleneck between lake and mountains, the corridor any army marching on Kyoto from the east would have to use. Naomasa died in 1602 of wounds taken at Sekigahara and his son Ii Naokatsu completed the castle in 1622. To save time and money the Ii pulled down the other fortresses in their territory and carted the pieces here: the three-storey keep came from Otsu Castle, the Tenbin turret from Nagahama, the Nishinomaru three-storey turret from Odani.

For the next two and a half centuries Hikone was the seat of the Ii, reckoned the foremost of the fudai daimyo, the hereditary Tokugawa vassals. Its best known lord was Ii Naosuke, who as tairo effectively governed Japan in the 1850s, signed the treaties that ended the country's seclusion, purged his opponents, and was cut down by Mito ronin outside Edo Castle's Sakurada Gate in 1860.

When the Meiji government ordered feudal fortifications demolished, Hikone was spared after the Emperor Meiji, touring the region, asked directly that it be kept. It therefore survives more completely than almost any other Japanese castle. The keep with its attached turrets is a National Treasure, one of only five so designated and one of the twelve original keeps still standing; the stables, the Tenbin turret, the Drum Gate and two further turret complexes are Important Cultural Properties. The daimyo palace was rebuilt in 1987 as the Hikone Castle Museum. Land reclamation has since left the castle roughly a kilometre back from the lake it once guarded.

Matsue Castle was built between 1607 and 1611 by Horio Yoshiharu, who had been granted Izumo and Oki with 240,000 koku after Sekigahara. He inherited the Amago clan's old mountain fastness at Gassan-Toda, judged it impractical for governing in peacetime, and moved his seat to Kameda, a hill of only 29 metres on the low ground between Lake Shinji and the Nakaumi lagoon, laying out a new castle town around it. The design is credited to Oze Hoan. Yoshiharu died in 1611, the year the work was finished. The Horio line failed in 1633 and the Kyogoku held Matsue briefly; from 1638 Matsudaira Naomasa, a grandson of Tokugawa Ieyasu transferred in from Matsumoto, began a tenure of ten generations that lasted until the Meiji Restoration. No siege was ever fought here. The castle was raised after the fighting had stopped, and its interest lies in being the administrative capital of Izumo rather than a battlefield.

The keep is the only original one surviving anywhere in the San'in region. It is a watchtower type tower roughly 30 metres tall, dark boarded, showing five roofs outside but six floors within, and it is one of just five keeps designated National Treasures, with Himeji, Matsumoto, Inuyama and Hikone. Under the Meiji abolition of castles the site went to the army and every building was to be sold off for demolition; local supporters bought the keep back and saved it, along with one attached turret and the stone walls. Prayer plaques dated to 1611 were found at Matsue Shrine in 2012 and fixed the construction date, which cleared the way for National Treasure status in July 2015. Several second bailey turrets were rebuilt in 2001 and the grounds are now a public park.

Maruoka stands on a low isolated hill in the Sakai plain north of Fukui, where the Hokurikudō met the road running inland to Mino. Oda Nobunaga crushed the Ikkō ikki rising in Echizen in 1575 and handed the province to Shibata Katsuie, whose nephew and adopted son Shibata Katsutoyo is traditionally said to have come down from Toyohara and raised this castle in 1576. Katsutoyo was moved to Nagahama after Nobunaga's death and died in 1583, the year Hideyoshi destroyed Katsuie at Kitanoshō. The Aoyama held Maruoka next, backed the losing Western army at Sekigahara in 1600 and were stripped of it. Ieyasu gave Echizen to his son Yūki Hideyasu, and from 1612 the castle went to Honda Narishige, at first as a guardian attached to Fukui and from the 1620s as daimyō of Maruoka in his own right; his heirs finished the castle and its town. The Honda were dispossessed after a succession quarrel in 1695, and the Arima held the domain until the han were abolished in 1871.

The small three storey keep is one of only twelve original keeps left in Japan and the only one in the Hokuriku region. It looks archaic, a watchtower with an open railed gallery set on a broad hipped roof, and was long advertised as the oldest keep in the country. That claim has collapsed. A survey commissioned by Sakai City, using tree ring dating and isotope analysis, reported in March 2019 that its main structural pillars come from timber felled after 1626, so the tower now standing is almost certainly a Honda rebuilding of the Kan'ei era, most likely 1628. Its roof tiles are cut from local shakudani stone rather than fired clay, a Hokuriku answer to snow and frost, which makes the roof extremely heavy. The keep fell down completely in the Fukui earthquake of 1948 when its base of rough uncut stone gave way, and was re-erected in 1955 around a concrete frame reusing most of its own fallen timbers. It is an Important Cultural Property, having been a National Treasure under the prewar law. The grounds are now Kasumigajō Park, planted with some 400 cherry trees; the pentagonal inner moat was filled in between late Taishō and early Shōwa, and two castle gates survive at temples in Awara and Komatsu.

Kōchi Castle stands on Ōtakasaka, a low hill in the middle of the Kōchi plain where two rivers meet. Chōsokabe Motochika began building here in the late 1580s, but the ground flooded and he moved his headquarters to Urado on the coast instead. After Sekigahara the Chōsokabe lost Tosa, and in 1601 the Tokugawa handed the province to Yamauchi Kazutoyo, a Kakegawa lord rewarded for backing Ieyasu. Kazutoyo judged Urado too cramped and too weak to hold a whole province, went back to the hill Motochika had given up on, and diked and drained the site. Work ran from 1601 to about 1611. The castle was first called Kawanakayama, the mountain among the rivers, and was renamed Kōchi soon after. His heirs governed Tosa from it until the domains were abolished in 1871, and the bad blood between the incoming Yamauchi retainers and the dispossessed Chōsokabe warriors shaped Tosa politics for the rest of the Edo period. A fire in 1727 burned almost the whole castle down. It was rebuilt between 1729 and 1753 to the old design rather than to a newer fashion, which is why the place still looks like a castle of about 1600. Kōchi then came through the Meiji demolitions and the wartime bombing of the city better than almost anywhere else in Japan. Its keep is one of only twelve that were never pulled down and replaced, and Kōchi is the only castle in the country that still has its keep and its honmaru palace, the Kaitokukan, standing together, with the gates, walls and storehouses of the inner enceinte around them. Fifteen structures are Important Cultural Properties and the grounds are a National Historic Site.

The hill above Uwajima Bay was fortified as early as the Heian period, against the pirate rebellion of Fujiwara no Sumitomo, and a branch of the Saionji family held the site through the Muromachi period until Chōsokabe Motochika overran southern Iyo. The castle standing today is essentially the work of Tōdō Takatora, the most inventive castle builder of his generation, who was given the district by Toyotomi Hideyoshi and rebuilt it between 1596 and about 1601. Takatora used an irregular five sided plan instead of the usual concentric rectangles, so that an attacker who worked out the line of one wall found the next one running away at an unexpected angle, and the sea originally came up to the eastern foot of the hill. After Takatora transferred to Imabari the castle passed briefly to Tomita Nobutaka, then in 1614 to Date Hidemune, eldest son of Date Masamune of Sendai. His line held Uwajima as a branch domain rated at a hundred thousand koku, reduced when a sub fief was split off at Iyo-Yoshida in 1657, and it produced Date Munenari, one of the reforming lords who shaped national politics in the 1860s. Earthquake damage in 1649 forced a long rebuilding, and in 1666 Hidemune's son Munetoshi put up the three storey keep that still stands. Uwajima never fell to an assault; its losses came in peacetime. Most of the outer walls, gates and turrets were cleared between 1900 and 1913 to enlarge the harbour, and the Ōtemon gate, made a National Treasure alongside the keep in 1934, burned in an American air raid in the closing weeks of the Pacific War. The Date family handed the keep and its grounds to the city in 1949. What survives is the original wooden keep, one of only twelve in Japan never rebuilt and now an Important Cultural Property, the Noboritachimon on the southern path up the hill, a rare large gate of its type protected as a city cultural property, and the stone walls of the inner bailey. The whole hill has been a National Historic Site since 1937.

Marugame stands on Kameyama, a low hill in western Sanuki near the Inland Sea coast of Shikoku. Toyotomi Hideyoshi granted the whole province to Ikoma Chikamasa in 1587; Chikamasa settled on Takamatsu as his seat and began a second castle here in the 1590s to hold western Sanuki, then passed it to his son Kazumasa. The Ikoma hedged their way through Sekigahara in 1600, the father backing the Western army and the son the Eastern, and kept the province. What they could not survive was the peace: the shogunate's one province, one castle edict of 1615 left Takamatsu standing and Marugame condemned. The site was revived in 1640, when the Ikoma were stripped of Sanuki after an internal revolt and the western districts went to Yamazaki Ieharu, a lord with a reputation for fortification who had worked on Osaka and Shimabara. He rebuilt Marugame on a scale well beyond what his small domain warranted. His line failed in 1658 and a cadet branch of the Kyogoku clan came in from Tatsuno in Harima; they raised the present keep in 1660, saw the works finished by 1670, and held Marugame Domain to the end of the Edo period.

The castle is remembered for its masonry rather than its buildings. Four tiers of wall climb roughly sixty metres from the foot of the hill to the top enclosure, the greatest stacked height of any castle in Japan, and each face swells outward at the base in the fan shaped curve masons called ogi no kobai. It is the clearest teaching example of how a hilltop was engineered rather than merely occupied. The three storey keep of 1660 survives, at about fifteen metres the smallest of Japan's twelve original keeps, along with the two gates of the main entrance; all are Important Cultural Properties, and the site has been a National Historic Site since 1953. Fire in 1869 destroyed the daimyo palace, the moats were filled from 1870, and army demolitions in 1876 took the turrets and much outer walling, but the keep and central baileys were spared and opened as Kameyama Park in 1919. A stretch of the outer stonework collapsed after the heavy rains and typhoon of 2018 and is being dismantled and relaid stone by stone, work expected to run into the late 2020s.

Matsuyama Castle stands on Mount Katsuyama, a 132 metre hill in the middle of the modern city. It was begun in 1602 by Kato Yoshiaki, who had made his name fighting for Toyotomi Hideyoshi at Shizugatake and then joined Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara, and was rewarded with the Iyo-Matsuyama domain of 200,000 koku. Yoshiaki moved his seat away from the old Kono country around Yuzuki and laid out a new hilltop fortress with a planned castle town beneath it. The work took a quarter of a century. Yoshiaki was transferred to Aizu just before completion in 1627, and it fell to Gamo Tadatomo to finish a five storey keep; Tadatomo died in 1634 without an heir, and the shogunate installed Matsudaira Sadayuki of the Hisamatsu-Matsudaira, a house reckoned kin to the Tokugawa, who held Matsuyama until 1868. Sadayuki rebuilt the keep smaller, at three storeys, in 1642. Lightning burned it in 1784, and the twelfth daimyo, Matsudaira Katsuyoshi, put it up again in 1854 using traditional carpentry, so the tower standing today is a late Edo building rather than a modern replica; it is one of only twelve original keeps left in Japan. It sits at the centre of a linked cluster of smaller towers and covered corridors, a plan it shares with Himeji and Wakayama. The Meiji government demolished most of the outer works, the army held the second and third baileys until 1945, eleven listed buildings burned in the Matsuyama air raid that year, and the Tsutsui Gate was lost to arson in 1949. Even so the keep, six turrets and a long sequence of original gates and walls survive, twenty one structures are Important Cultural Properties, and the site has been a National Historic Site since 1952.

Hirosaki was the seat of the Tsugaru, a family that broke away from its Nambu overlords in the 1580s. Ōura Tamenobu was rewarded by Toyotomi Hideyoshi for his part in the Odawara campaign of 1590 and took the Tsugaru surname at that time, then backed Tokugawa Ieyasu at Sekigahara and was confirmed as lord of Hirosaki Domain at 47,000 koku. He began the castle in 1603 but died in Kyoto the following year; his son Nobuhira resumed the work in 1609, stripping the older Horikoshi and Ōura castles of gates and timber to speed it along, and finished in 1611. It is a hirayamajiro on a low rise, laid out in six concentric baileys behind wide moats, roughly 600 metres east to west and 950 metres north to south. The original five-storey keep stood only sixteen years: lightning struck it in 1627 and it burned. The domain was too poor, and too wary of arousing shogunal suspicion, to replace it for nearly two centuries. The present three-storey keep, 14.4 metres tall, was raised in 1810 by the ninth daimyo Tsugaru Yasuchika on a corner turret base at the southeast rather than on the original southwest foundation. Hirosaki was never attacked. The Tsugaru surrendered it intact in 1871 and gave the grounds over as a public park in 1895, which is why so much survives: the 1810 keep, three Edo period corner turrets, five gates and a guardhouse, all National Important Cultural Properties standing on a National Historic Site. It is the northernmost of Japan's twelve surviving original keeps and the only one in Tōhoku. In 2015 the whole keep was jacked up and rolled some 70 metres inland so that the bulging stone wall beneath it could be dismantled and rebuilt, and the return move to its old base is under way in 2026.

A small fort stood here from the 1520s, held for the Imagawa until Oda Nobuhide seized it in 1532; some accounts make it Nobunaga's birthplace. It had been derelict for a generation when Tokugawa Ieyasu ordered a great new castle on the spot in 1609 and made other lords pay for it. Twenty daimyo, many of them former enemies such as Kato Kiyomasa and Fukushima Masanori, were each assigned stretches of wall and gate under the compulsory service called tenka bushin, work that drained their treasuries while binding them publicly to the new regime. The stone bases were done in 1610, the great keep in 1612, the Honmaru palace in 1615. Ieyasu then closed down nearby Kiyosu and moved the entire town, its garrison, temples, merchants and even its buildings, to the new site in the wholesale relocation remembered as the Kiyosu-goshi; Kiyosu's keep was re-erected here as the northwest turret. The castle became the seat of Ieyasu's ninth son Yoshinao and of the Owari Tokugawa, senior of the three cadet houses from which a shogun could be drawn, and the town below grew into a major stop between the Tokaido and the Nakasendo. Its keep carried a celebrated pair of gilded shachihoko, dolphin-shaped roof ornaments so valuable that the domain melted and recast them three times to raise cash.

The Owari house submitted to the imperial side in 1868 without fighting, and the castle escaped Meiji demolition partly after foreign protests, including one from the German minister. Nagoya city took it over in 1930 and 24 buildings were declared national treasures, but an American incendiary raid on 14 May 1945 burned the great and small keeps, the Honmaru palace and the golden dolphins. Three corner turrets, several gates, the moats and the vast stone walls are original. The keep that dominates the site today is a 1959 concrete replica, shut to visitors since 2018 over earthquake safety, and the city intends to rebuild it in timber. The Honmaru palace was recreated in wood and fully opened in 2018, its Kano school wall paintings copied from surviving originals.

The site was first fortified not by a warlord but by a church. From the late fifteenth century the Ikkō-ikki, the militant congregations of the Jōdo Shinshū sect who followed the preaching of Rennyo, pushed aside the Togashi governors of Kaga and ran the province themselves. Their headquarters was the Kanazawa Gobō, a fortified temple complex on the tip of the Kodatsuno ridge between the Sai and Asano rivers. Oda Nobunaga's armies broke that arrangement, and in 1580 his general Sakuma Morimasa seized the temple site, was granted the province and began laying out the moats and baileys. Morimasa was defeated in 1583 and Maeda Toshiie took his place. Toshiie ordered a complete rebuilding in 1592 with the help of a Christian daimyō known for castle design, generally identified as Takayama Ukon, who was then living under Maeda protection. Kanazawa became the seat of the Kaga domain, assessed at over a million koku and by far the largest holding under the Tokugawa, and fourteen generations of Maeda ruled from it until 1871. Much of the castle's later history is a history of fire. The keep burned in 1602 and was never rebuilt; further fires in 1631 and 1759 swept away most of what stood, so the buildings on the site belong to repeated Edo period reconstruction rather than to the Sengoku castle. The whitish roofs are a Kanazawa signature: the tiles are lead, chosen because they do not burn, though local legend adds that they could be melted into bullets under siege. Original fabric survives in the Ishikawa Gate of 1788, the long Sanjikken Nagaya storehouse and the Tsurumaru Storehouse, all Important Cultural Properties. The army took the grounds in 1871 for the headquarters of its Ninth Division, Kanazawa University occupied part of them from 1949 to 1989, and since then the prefecture has run a patient programme of timber reconstruction using traditional joinery: the Hishi Yagura turret, Gojikken Nagaya and Hashizume-mon turret in 2001, the Kahoku Gate in 2010, the Hashizume Gate in 2015 and the Nezumita Gate in 2020. The site is now Kanazawa Castle Park, across the road from Kenrokuen garden.

Date Masamune moved his seat here after Sekigahara, laying out the ground on Mount Aoba in the winter of 1600 with Tokugawa Ieyasu's permission and renaming the place Sendai. The hill had carried earlier forts, including the Kokubun clan's Chiyo Castle, from which the name Sendai is said to derive. Masamune chose it for its defences and for its position where the coast road and the mountain road met; the inner bailey sits about 115 metres up, closed off by cliffs to the south and east, by the Hirose river to the north, and by stone revetments as much as 15 metres high. He had a keep platform built but never raised a keep on it, relying instead on four three storey turrets and a lavish Momoyama style residence. That restraint is usually read as prudence toward a Tokugawa regime that watched the Date closely, and it makes Sendai a telling counterpoint to the tower building of the previous generation; the Spanish envoy Sebastian Vizcaino still judged it one of the strongest places in Japan. Masamune's son Tadamune completed the works and in 1639 moved the lord's residence down to a new second bailey at the foot of the hill, from which the domain was actually governed for the rest of the Edo period. The castle was never attacked. Even in the Boshin War, when Date Yoshikuni headed the northern alliance against the new imperial government, Sendai surrendered without a fight. The army took the site in 1871, fire destroyed the second bailey buildings in 1882, and the great gate with its flanking turret, National Treasures since 1931, burned in the American air raid of 10 July 1945. What survives is earthwork and stone: ramparts, moats and the tall inner bailey walls, repaired again after the 2011 earthquake. The turret beside the gate is a 1967 reconstruction, and the only original castle gate now stands elsewhere in the city, reused as the entrance to the Miyagi governor's residence. The ruins were designated a National Historic Site in 2003.

Hagi Castle was the consolation prize of a defeat. Mōri Terumoto backed the losing side at Sekigahara in 1600, and although his army never actually fought, Tokugawa Ieyasu stripped the Mōri of two thirds of their lands, including their home province of Aki and their new castle at Hiroshima, leaving them only Nagato and Suō. The Mōri asked to build a new seat at Yamaguchi or Hōfu, both on the Sanyōdō highway running from Kyoto towards Kyushu, but the shogunate refused and sent them instead to Hagi, at that time a fishing village on the Sea of Japan coast, hemmed in by hills and river marsh and far from any road that mattered. Work began in 1604 and finished in 1608. The citadel sat on Mount Shizuki, a 150 metre former island at the tip of the Abu river delta, with two walled enclosures on the sandbank below, the open sea serving as a moat on one side and a sea fed water moat on the other, and a five storey keep at the corner of the main enclosure. No army ever besieged it. Hagi matters politically rather than militarily: for more than 250 years it was the seat of Chōshū domain, whose samurai became the most dangerous enemies the shogunate had in the 1860s. In 1863, after the Shimonoseki fighting showed how exposed the coast was to foreign warships, the Mōri moved their government inland to Yamaguchi, and in 1874 the new Meiji government had the castle buildings pulled down. What survives is the ground plan in stone: the walls of the hilltop and of the main enclosure are largely intact, along with the water moat, and a gate and a corner turret have since been rebuilt. The ruins are a National Historic Site, the samurai quarter below is protected as a preserved castle town, and since 2015 the site has formed part of a UNESCO World Heritage listing.

Built as the family temple of the Soga clan, Asuka-dera (also Hōkō-ji) was the first Buddhist foundation in Japan to have a fully-fledged temple complex; the Nihon Shoki has Soga no Umako vow to raise it after defeating the anti-Buddhist Mononobe, records craftsmen and monks despatched from Baekje in 588, and notes its completion in 596. Its principal image, a bronze Shaka triad attributed to Kuratsukuri no Tori and finished between about 606 and 609, survives as the Asuka Daibutsu and is an Important Cultural Property. Primarily a Sanron centre, the temple drew immigrant clergy from Baekje, Goguryeo and China and functioned in effect as a research institute for Buddhist doctrine, which earned it imperial protection and let it outlive the destruction of the Soga in the Isshi Incident of 645. When the capital shifted to Heijō-kyō the institution moved with it and became Gangō-ji, while the Asuka site continued as Hon-Gangō-ji; it lost its pagoda and main hall to lightning in 1196 and was practically abandoned after the Muromachi period, its main image left standing in the open air by 1447. Excavation since 1956 has recovered the original one-pagoda, three-golden-hall plan, the present main hall of 1826 stands exactly on the site of the Central Golden Hall, and the precincts have been a National Historic Site since 1966.

descriptions.value: Tōdai-ji was founded in 738 and opened in 752 as head of the provincial temple (kokubunji) network decreed by Emperor Shōmu in 741, after smallpox, failed harvests and the Fujiwara no Hirotsugu rebellion convinced him that state Buddhism might shield the realm. The colossal bronze Vairocana (Birushana) was commissioned in 743, built in eight castings over three years, completed in 751 and consecrated the following year at an eye-opening ceremony attended by 10,000 monks and 4,000 dancers, the rite performed by the Indian priest Bodhisena; temple records claim more than 2,600,000 people contributed rice, timber, metal, cloth or labour. Under the Ritsuryō state the temple housed offices of all six Nara schools and every officially licensed monk took ordination here, Kūkai and Saichō among them, until the Vinaya lineage lapsed. The Daibutsuden has been rebuilt twice after fire, once from around 1180 in Southern Song fashion under abbot Shunjōbō Chōgen and again in 1709; the present hall is roughly 30 percent smaller than its predecessor, reduced from eleven bays to seven for want of funds, while the late twelfth-century Nandaimon still shelters the 8.5-metre Niō carved by Unkei, Kaikei and their workshop. Today it is the Japanese headquarters of the Kegon school, its storehouse the Shōsōin holds Tenpyō-period treasures, and its Kon-dō, Nandaimon, Hokke-dō, Nigatsu-dō and other halls are National Treasures within the UNESCO Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara.

descriptions.value: Kōfuku-ji began in 669 as a private vow by Kagami-no-Ōkimi, wife of Fujiwara no Kamatari, who prayed for her husband's recovery from illness; originally sited at Yamashina, it was moved to Fujiwara-kyō in 672 and dismantled a second time in 710 to be re-erected east of the new capital at Heijō-kyō. Kamatari's son Fujiwara no Fuhito named it after the Vimalakīrti Sūtra, and as the Fujiwara tutelary temple and national headquarters of the East Asian Yogācāra (Hossō) school it prospered with the family, retaining influence over the imperial government by aggressive means in some cases and keeping its standing among the Nanto Shichi Daiji even after rivals such as Tōdai-ji declined once the court moved to Heian-kyō. Empress Kōmyō, Fuhito's daughter and consort of Emperor Shōmu, ordered the five-storied pagoda in 730 and the Saikondō in 734, and the Fusō Ryakuki credits her with endowing Japan's first medical dispensary and welfare institution here. Civil war and fire wrecked the complex repeatedly; the Nandaimon, Chūmon, corridor and one of the three golden halls were never replaced, and the Central Golden Hall was only rebuilt in 2018. What remains is nonetheless exceptional: the Three-storied Pagoda of 1185, the Hoku'endō of 1210, the Tō-kondō of 1425 and the Five-storied Pagoda of 1426 are all National Treasures, as are the dry-lacquer Ashura among the Devas of the Eight Classes and the Ten Principal Disciples, and the temple forms part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara.

Saichō (767 to 822), known posthumously as Dengyō Daishi, founded Enryaku-ji on Mount Hiei in 788 after bringing the Tendai teaching from China, and with Emperor Kanmu's support ordained a hundred disciples in 807 under a discipline that kept monks secluded on the mountain for twelve years of study and meditation before the ablest were retained or released into government service. The mountain became the seminary of medieval Japanese Buddhism, since the founders of Jōdo-shū, Jōdo Shinshū, Sōtō Zen and Nichiren Buddhism all spent time there. At its height the complex numbered as many as 3,000 sub-temples and an army of warrior monks (sōhei); a tenth-century succession quarrel between the lines of Ennin and Enchin split Tendai into the Mountain Order (sanmon) at Enryaku-ji and the Temple Order (jimon) at Mii-dera, after which the leadership hired mercenary armies that intimidated rivals and even marched on the capital to force monastic demands. Oda Nobunaga ended that militancy in 1571 by levelling the buildings and slaughtering the monks, and only the thirteenth-century Ruri-dō survived; the present structures date from the late sixteenth to the mid-seventeenth century, the main hall rebuilt in 1642 under Tokugawa Iemitsu, with some halls brought in from other temples, notably Mii-dera. The buildings cluster in three precincts, Tō-dō, Sai-tō and Yokokawa, and the monastery remains the Tendai headquarters, the centre of the kaihōgyō practice of the "marathon monks", and part of the UNESCO Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.

descriptions.value: Founded in 672 at the foot of Mount Hiei near Lake Biwa, in the aftermath of the succession war that placed Emperor Tenmu on the throne, Nagara-san Onjō-ji was raised in memory of the emperor's brother, Tenji; the familiar name Mii-dera ("Temple of Three Wells") came nearly two centuries later from the abbot Enchin, after the springs used there for the ritual bathing of newborns. Under Enchin's leadership (859 to 891) it came to stand beside Tōdai-ji, Kōfuku-ji and Enryaku-ji as one of the four temples charged with protecting the capital, but his death opened a lasting rift within Tendai: Mii-dera became head of the Jimon branch against Enryaku-ji's Sanmon, a rivalry more geographic than doctrinal yet violent enough that Enryaku-ji's sōhei burned Mii-dera to the ground four times in the eleventh century alone. Its warrior-monks acted as political players in their own right, sheltering Prince Mochihito in June 1180 and marching with the Minamoto to the Byōdō-in, for which Taira no Kiyomori ordered the temple destroyed; much of the complex fell again to Oda Nobunaga's army in 1571. The present Kondō dates from 1599 and still houses a spring of sacred water, the Kannon-dō from 1072, and the Kōjō-in Kyakuden of 1601 is a National Treasure and a model of late Muromachi shoin-zukuri, decorated with fusuma by Kanō Sanraku. Some forty named buildings survive; the temple is station 14 on the Saigoku Kannon pilgrimage, and its bronze evening bell carries a body of legend, including a tale of the sōhei Benkei.

Kongōbu-ji, the "Temple of the Diamond Mountain Peak", is the ecclesiastical head temple of Kōyasan Shingon Buddhism, seated on the high plateau of Mount Kōya that Kūkai settled in 819 and where the original monastery grew into the temple town of Kōya. The building a visitor enters today is not Kūkai's: it was raised in 1593 as Seigan-ji by Toyotomi Hideyoshi on the death of his mother, rebuilt in 1861, and given its present name only in 1869. Its interiors are hung with sliding doors (fusuma) painted by Kanō Tanyū (1602 to 1674) and members of the Kyoto Kanō school, while the modern Banryūtei is the largest rock garden in Japan at 2,340 square metres, its 140 granite stones set to suggest a pair of dragons rising from cloud to guard the temple. The temple remains a working seat of authority rather than a museum piece: its 414th abbot serves at the same time as archbishop of the Kōyasan Shingon school, and visitors may hear the monks' sermons and join sessions of ajikan, the Shingon practice of meditating on the letter A written in the Siddhaṃ script. Kōyasan, Kongōbu-ji included, was inscribed by UNESCO in 2004 within the "Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range".

Tō-ji, the "East Temple", was founded in 796, two years after the court moved to Heian-kyō, and was one of only three Buddhist temples permitted in the new capital; it alone survives, its partner Sai-ji having faded away in the sixteenth century through poor irrigation in Ukyō-ku and want of funds. Its formal name, Kyō-ō-gokoku-ji, states the purpose plainly: defence of the nation by means of the King of Doctrines, and that charge took esoteric form in 823, when Emperor Saga placed the temple in Kūkai's hands, from which time it has been a Shingon foundation with Yakushi Nyorai as its principal image. Tō-ji declined at the close of the Heian period and returned to prominence in the Kamakura period on the strength of Daishi shinkō, the cult of Kūkai himself, whose residence is commemorated by the Miedō. Five of its buildings are National Treasures in two categories: the Lotus Flower Gate (rengemon), the Miedō, the Kondō (which holds a Yakushi of 1603) and the five-storey pagoda, together with the Kanchi-in guest hall; the pagoda, at 54.8 metres the tallest wooden tower in Japan, was rebuilt in 1643 by order of the third Tokugawa shōgun, Iemitsu, after four earlier losses, and was itself designated a National Treasure in 1952. Tō-ji was inscribed by UNESCO in 1994 among the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto, and on the twenty-first of each month, the day of Kūkai's death in 835, the grounds fill with the Kōbō-san market.

descriptions.value: Ise Jingū, known simply as Jingū, is the holiest site in Shinto: a complex of some 125 shrines centred on the Naikū (Kōtai Jingū), dedicated to the sun goddess Amaterasu Ōmikami, and the Gekū (Toyouke Daijingū), dedicated to the deity of agriculture and food, Toyouke-hime. Tradition following the Nihon Shoki dates the Naikū to 4 BCE and ascribes its siting to Yamatohime-no-mikoto, daughter of Emperor Suinin, who wandered for twenty years from Mount Miwa through Ōmi and Mino until Amaterasu named Ise as the secluded land where she wished to dwell; third and fifth century datings have also been proposed, and the first shrine building at Naikū is credited to Emperor Tenmu, with the first ceremonial rebuilding carried out by Empress Jitō in 692. That rebuilding became the Shikinen Sengū, the twenty-year renewal expressing tokowaka, in which the shrines and the Uji Bridge are dismantled and rebuilt on an adjacent site by miyadaiku carpenters working without power tools; the present buildings, the 62nd iteration, date from 2013 and cost 57 billion yen (about US$550 million) raised from private donations alone, with the next renewal due in 2033. The architecture is yuitsu-shinmei-zukuri, a variant that may be used for no other shrine and that echoes ancient raised rice granaries: hinoki cypress joined without nails, pillars set directly into the ground, and a thatched reed roof carrying ten katsuogi and chigi cut flat on top to mark a female deity. Ise's standing was political as well as ritual, served from the late seventh century to the fourteenth by a Saiō, an imperial princess as high priestess, and drawing mass pilgrimage in the Edo period (okage mairi), when 3.62 million people are recorded as visiting in fifty days in 1625; the shrine is held to house the sacred mirror Yata no Kagami, and the public is still admitted no further than sight of the thatched roofs behind four tall tamagaki fences.

No record gives the date of Izumo-taisha's establishment; the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki account for it mythologically, as the dwelling Amaterasu presented to Ōkuninushi after he ceded his country to her grandson Ninigi-no-Mikoto, and the shrine is widely regarded as the oldest in Japan, predating Ise. Its main hall gives its name to taisha-zukuri, the oldest style of shrine building, with an off-centre entrance, nine support pillars dividing the interior into four sections and enormous scissor-shaped chigi on the roof; a record compiled around 950 describes a hall of roughly 48 metres, taller than the 45-metre hall of the Great Buddha at Tōdai-ji, and the discovery in 2000 of the remains of enormous pillars lends credence to that tradition. The structure was reduced in size around 1200, in the Kamakura period, and rebuilt in 1744 at its present 24 metres, by which time easier travel was turning Izumo into a central place of pilgrimage; renewal follows a sengū cycle of some 60 to 70 years, the deity having been moved for renovation in 1809, 1881 and 1953 and returned to the inner shrine before more than 8,000 people on 11 May 2013. Ōkuninushi is venerated as the deity of marriage and the god who establishes good relationships, and in the tenth lunar month the gods are believed to gather here to settle the coming year's marriages, deaths and births, so the Izumo region calls that month kamiarizuki (the month with gods) while the rest of Japan calls it kannazuki (the month without gods). The honden and attached buildings were designated National Treasures in 1952; visitors today pass the Kagura-den, hung with the largest shimenawa in Japan at 13.5 metres and about five tonnes, and the Shōkokan museum of treasures, while the Senge family, descendants of Amenohohi-no-mikoto who bore the title Izumo Kokusō, lost the administration when the shrine was ranked a Kanpei-taisha in 1871 and recovered it after the war, Takatoshi Senge becoming chief priest in 1947.

descriptions.value: Kasuga-taisha was established in 768 as the shrine of the Fujiwara family, its foundation legend telling how the first kami, Takemikazuchi, rode from Kashima Jingū on the back of a white deer to the summit of Mount Mikasa to protect Nara; imperial favour followed in the Nara period through Fujiwara influence and that of Empress Shōtoku, and from 1871 to 1946 the shrine ranked among the Kanpei-taisha, the first tier of government-supported shrines. Four kami are enshrined in four halls of identical form (Takemikazuchi, Futsunushi, Ame-no-Koyane and the consort Himegami), worshipped collectively as Kasuga Daimyōjin, a composite deity read through honji suijaku, the theory identifying Buddhist divinities with kami counterparts, which allowed a worshipper to address several gods at once. The sanctuary gave its name to the Kasuga-zukuri style, marked by sloping gabled roofs, katsuogi and chigi, and the complex, enclosed by four cloisters and holding a treasure house of hundreds of national treasures and other cultural properties (mostly Heian works, including gagaku drums and bronze mirrors), maintains shikinen zōtai, rebuilding to identical specifications every twenty years since the Nara period, the sixtieth renewal falling in 2016. Over three thousand stone and bronze lanterns line the approach and hang along the corridors; they are lit together only at Setsubun Mantōrō on 3 February and Chūgen Mantōrō on 14 and 15 August, while the auxiliary Wakamiya Jinja, founded in 1135, is the focus of the Kasuga Wakamiya festival each December. Hunting and logging have been forbidden on Kasugayama since 841, leaving the forest backdrop essentially unchanged since the Nara period, and the shrine together with the Kasugayama Primeval Forest is registered by UNESCO as part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara, its freely roaming deer still regarded as sacred messengers of the gods.

descriptions.value: Shrine tradition places the foundation in the first year of Empress Suiko (593), when the local chieftain Saeki Kuramoto is said to have raised a hall on the island for the three daughters of Susanoo (Ichikishimahime, Tagorihime and Tagitsuhime), the sanjoshin or three female deities of seas and storms; Itsukushima served as the ichinomiya, or chief shrine, of Aki Province. Its present form is owed to Taira no Kiyomori, who as governor of Aki contributed heavily to its construction from 1168 and ordered the main hall built in reverence for the tutelary god of navigation, making Miyajima the Taira clan shrine and a base for the family's maritime activity and its attempted monopoly of the Inland Sea trade with Song China; the Taira dedicated the celebrated Heike Nōkyō, thirty-two scrolls of the Lotus, Amida and Heart sutras copied by Kiyomori, his sons and other kinsmen and decorated with gold, silver and mother-of-pearl. Because the island itself was held to be a god and no births or deaths were allowed to pollute it, the shrine was built like a pier over the water in Shinden-zukuri style so that it appeared to float, separate from the land, and commoners had to steer their boats through the torii before approaching; the prohibition still stands, with no births or deaths permitted near the shrine since 1878. Later patrons continued the work: Mōri Motonari, who was said to have tainted the island's sacred ground by fighting Sue Takafusa there in 1555, rebuilt the honden in 1571, and a Noh stage extending from the haraiden dates to 1590, while the vermilion ōtorii of decay-resistant camphor wood, about 15 metres tall and given extra legs before and behind each pillar in the Ryōbu Shintō manner, stands in its present form from 1875 though a gate has occupied the spot since 1168. Typhoon Songda badly damaged the boardwalks and roof on 5 September 2004 and closed the shrine for repairs; it was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1996, several of its buildings and possessions are designated National Treasures, and the Kangen-sai boat ritual initiated by Kiyomori is still performed each summer.

Kumano Hongū Taisha in Tanabe, Wakayama Prefecture, is the shrine to which all the ancient Kumano Kodō routes lead, and it enshrines the Kumano Sansho Gongen: Ketsumimiko, Hayatama and Fusubi. A pilgrim writing more than nine hundred years ago described a vast precinct of five main pavilions housing twelve deities, ringed by numerous lesser shrines and temples; fire and flood damaged it repeatedly over the centuries and it was always rebuilt to its original state, so faithfully that the reconstruction of 1803, following the last fire of 1776, is almost identical to a drawing of the grounds made some eight hundred years ago. The shrine stood until modern times at Ōyunohara, a sandbank at the confluence of the Kumano and Otonashi rivers, but a flood in 1889 partly destroyed it and the surviving buildings were moved to the present hillside site in 1891, where only three of the five pavilions were rebuilt; four deities were brought across and the remaining eight are still enshrined at Ōyunohara in two stone monuments. The halls are built of natural unfinished materials, roofed in hinoki cypress bark and jointed without nails, with bronze chigi and katsuogi crowning a thick roof that sweeps forward over the steps, and the sheltered corridor beneath the verandas, where pilgrims and ascetics once meditated, copied sutras, performed austerities and slept, and where Ippen Shōnin is said to have attained enlightenment, has earned the buildings their own designation as Kumano style, a mixture of the Kasuga and Taisha forms. Since 2000 the entrance to the old sandbank has been marked by the Ōtorii, at 33.9 metres high and 42 metres wide the largest torii gate in the world, made of steel weighing 172 tonnes; the shrine is included with the rest of the Kumano Sanzan in the World Heritage Site Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range, and the three-legged crow Yatagarasu is honoured at the Yata-no-Hi fire festival held at Ōyunohara on the last Saturday of August.

The site began as Kitayama-dai, the villa of the courtier Saionji Kintsune, until the shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu bought it from the Saionji family in 1397 and remade it as his Kitayama retirement estate; on his death it was converted, according to his own wishes, into a Zen temple officially named Rokuon-ji. The pavilion itself, believed to have been built in 1399, is a shariden housing relics of the Buddha, and it stacks three architectural idioms one above another: the Heian aristocratic shinden-zukuri of the ground floor (Hō-sui-in), the warrior buke-zukuri of the second, which holds a Buddha hall and a shrine to Kannon (Chō-on-dō), and Chinese-derived Zen zenshū-butsuden-zukuri at the top (Kukkyō-chō), the upper two storeys sheathed in gold leaf beneath a bronze hōō finial. It sits in a kaiyū-shiki strolling garden laid out after descriptions of Amida's Western Paradise, its reflection carried on the Kyōko-chi or Mirror Pond, borrowing the surrounding scenery (shakkei) in the manner that makes the Muromachi period a classical age of Japanese garden design. Every building in the complex except the pavilion burned during the Ōnin War (1467 to 1477), and the pavilion in turn was destroyed on 2 July 1950 by a twenty-two-year-old novice, Hayashi Shōken, an episode fictionalised in Mishima Yukio's novel of 1956. What stands today is the reconstruction of 1955, regilded in 1986 and 1987 with gold leaf far thicker than the original; the temple is a National Special Historic Site and one of the seventeen Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto inscribed by UNESCO.

Ashikaga Yoshimasa was planning a retirement villa at the foot of the Higashiyama hills as early as 1460, furnishing it with stones and pines carried off from the Flowery Palace and the Muromachi Hall after civil war had wrecked them, and construction of its two-storeyed Kannon-den began on 21 February 1482. He meant the building to answer the golden pavilion raised by his grandfather Ashikaga Yoshimitsu and intended to sheathe it in silver foil, but the Ōnin War halted the work and the covering was never applied; the nickname Ginkaku, Silver Pavilion, is in fact no older than the Edo period, and the unfinished surface is now read as an emblem of wabi-sabi. Yoshimasa took Buddhist vows in 1485 and is said to have sat in the pavilion contemplating the gardens while Kyoto burned, and on his death on 27 January 1490 the villa became a Zen temple named Jishō-ji after his Buddhist name; it belongs today to the Shōkoku-ji branch of Rinzai Zen. The complex is one of the defining monuments of Higashiyama bunka, the cultural flowering that Yoshimasa's patronage set in motion, although its garden was financed by the shogunate as a retreat for aesthetic enjoyment rather than laid out by monks for zazen. Visitors now walk wooded, deeply mossed grounds and a garden traditionally attributed to Sōami, with a sand garden whose carefully formed cone is said to stand for Mount Fuji; the restoration begun in February 2008 deliberately left the silver foil unapplied and the lacquer unrenewed.

descriptions.value: The ground was religious long before the temple: Empress Tachibana no Kachiko, wife of Emperor Saga, founded Danrin-ji here in the early Heian period, and it was here that the monk Gikū taught Zen in Japan for the first time, though his teaching found little welcome and the site fell into four centuries of decay before Emperor Go-Saga and his son Emperor Kameyama rebuilt it in the mid-thirteenth century as the Kameyama Detached Palace. Ashikaga Takauji had the palace converted into a temple in 1339 to hold memorial services for Emperor Go-Daigo, the former friend turned enemy who had decreed his execution after the failed Kenmu Restoration, and he had the Zen monk Musō Soseki build it and serve as its first chief priest; the intended name Ryakuō Shiseizen-ji was set aside after Takauji's younger brother Tadayoshi dreamed of a golden dragon over the Ōi River, and the finished temple was dedicated in 1345 at a ceremony that doubled as Go-Daigo's memorial. Its finances were commercial as much as devotional: two trading vessels, the Tenryūji-bune, were launched in 1342 to raise building funds, and in the 1430s the temple entered a tributary relationship with Ming China under which formal trade could proceed in exchange for Chinese control over the succession of its abbots, giving Tenryū-ji something near a monopoly on Japan's legitimate China trade, a circuit its priests helped coordinate between China, Okinawa and Japan into the nineteenth century. Ranked first among Kyoto's Five Mountains (Gozan), it grew to roughly 330,000 square metres and is said once to have held some 150 sub-temples, but it burned six times in the medieval period (1358, 1367, 1373, 1380, 1447 and 1467), was destroyed again in the Ōnin War, lost to fire once more in 1815 and severely damaged in the Kinmon Incident of 1864, so that almost every building now standing is a late Meiji reconstruction. The Momoyama-style Chokushi gate is the oldest structure on the grounds, a cloud dragon (Unryū-zu) by Suzuki Shōnen covers the ceiling of the lecture hall rebuilt in 1900, and Musō Soseki's garden circling Sōgen Pond, a Special Place of Scenic Beauty, preserves only traces of its original design; the temple was inscribed by UNESCO in 1994 among the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.

descriptions.value: Shōkoku-ji, formally Mannen-zan Shōkoku Shōten Zenji, was founded in 1382 by the shōgun Ashikaga Yoshimitsu; work on the central halls began in 1383 and the complex was dedicated in 1392, marked by a banquet for the great officers of the imperial court and the military leaders of the day whose pomp was said to equal an imperial occasion. Yoshimitsu designated the Zen master Shun'oku Myōha founding abbot in 1383, but Myōha insisted that the honour be accorded posthumously to his own teacher Musō Soseki, a decision formally proclaimed in 1385. Fire destroyed the entire complex in 1394 and Yoshimitsu financed its rebuilding, the first of many reconstructions, notably during the Ōnin War; later patrons included Toyotomi Hideyoshi, Toyotomi Hideyori and Tokugawa Ieyasu, with Hideyori paying for the 1605 rebuilding of the Hattō (Dharma Hall), Ieyasu donating the Sanmon in 1609, and Emperor Go-Mizunoo giving an imperial palace building to serve as the Kaisandō, the Founder's Hall. The conflagration of 1788 devastated the complex once more but spared that seventeenth-century Hattō, which survives as an Important Cultural Property and the oldest building of its type in Japan; its slightly domed ceiling carries a dragon by Kanō Mitsunobu, symbol of the rain of Buddhist teachings, and a handclap on the stone floor below returns as a rolling echo. Ranked second among the Kyoto Gozan, and briefly first in 1392, Shōkoku-ji is today the headquarters of one of the fourteen autonomous branches of Rinzai Zen, with more than ninety affiliated temples including the Golden and Silver Pavilions, and it houses the Jōtenkaku Museum on its grounds.

descriptions.value: Emperor Kameyama founded Nanzen-ji, formerly Zenrin-ji, in 1291 on the site of his own detached palace in the eastern hills of Kyoto, and it remains the headquarters of the Nanzen-ji branch of Rinzai Zen. It was never counted among the five great Zen temples of the Kyoto Gozan, yet it presided over them: once Ashikaga Yoshimitsu completed Shōkoku-ji in 1386 the ranking was revised to set Nanzen-ji above the whole system in a class of its own, titled First Temple of the Land and charged with a supervising role over the network. Fire took the complex in 1393, 1447 and 1467; it was rebuilt in 1597 and enlarged in the Edo period, its sub-temples fluctuating over time between nine and twelve. The Sanmon a visitor passes today was first raised in the 13th century, pulled down by government order in 1369 and rebuilt in 1628, and its elevated gallery supplied the setting for the thief Ishikawa Goemon's celebrated speech in the kabuki play Sanmon Gosan no Kiri of 1778. Behind it stands the hōjō or abbot's quarters, a National Treasure presented by Emperor Go-Yōzei and hung with Kanō Tan'yū's gold-ground tigers, fronted by Kobori Enshū's karesansui garden of the early 1600s (a designated Place of Scenic Beauty), while a brick aqueduct of 1890 carries Lake Biwa Canal water straight through the precinct.

descriptions.value: Kenchō-ji was completed in 1253, the fifth year of the Kenchō era from which it takes its name, built on the orders of Emperor Go-Fukakusa and at the invitation of the regent Hōjō Tokiyori, who summoned the Song Chinese master Lanxi Daolong (Rankei Dōryū) to lead it; it is the oldest Zen training monastery in Japan and ranks first among the Kamakura Gozan. Tokiyori's patronage was devotional and political at once, for the Five Mountain network that Kenchō-ji headed operated as a de facto ministry, circulating shogunal law, monitoring provincial conditions and supplying the Hōjō and later the Ashikaga with translators, diplomats and advisers behind a religious mask. Under that patronage the Gozan temples became centres of learning and produced the Literature of the Five Mountains, whose scholars reached far into national politics before the system decayed along with the Ashikaga shogunate; Kenchō-ji's own revival waited until the 19th century and the Zen master Aozora Kandō. Most of the original shichidō garan and its forty-nine subtemples burned in the fires of the 14th and 15th centuries, leaving ten subtemples today, though the surviving halls still stand in the classic Zen alignment from north to south. A visitor moves past the Sanmon of 1754, nicknamed Tanuki-mon after the raccoon dog said to have raised its funds disguised as a monk, the National Treasure bell cast in 1255, the Butsuden and Karamon brought from Zōjō-ji in 1647, and the Hattō of 1814, the largest wooden Buddhist structure in eastern Japan, before reaching the Shin-ji Ike pond garden attributed to Musō Soseki and the hillside shrine of Hansōbō, brought here in 1890.

descriptions.value: Engaku-ji was founded in 1282 by the Chinese master Mugaku Sōgen (1226 to 1286) at the request of the Kamakura regent Hōjō Tokimune, a long-committed patron of Zen who had just repelled the Mongol invasions of 1274 and 1281 and wanted a temple to honour the dead of both sides while serving as a centre from which Zen could spread. Its name comes from a copy of the Sutra of Perfect Enlightenment (engaku-kyō) said to have been dug from the hillside in a stone chest as building began. Ranked second among the Kamakura Gozan, the complex keeps the classical Zen monastic plan, its eighteen temples climbing a wooded slope with the major halls set in a straight perpendicular line; its present form is largely the work of the priest Seisetsu Shucho (1745 to 1820), who rebuilt and consolidated the site around the 500th anniversary of the founding in 1785. Two National Treasures anchor the precinct: the Shariden, a reliquary hall in karayō or Zenshū-yō style close to Song models, moved here from the Taiheiji convent after the original of 1285 burned in 1563 and said to hold a tooth of Shakyamuni presented to Minamoto no Sanetomo, and the Great Bell (Ōgane) cast in 1301 by Mononobe Kunimitsu at the order of Hōjō Sadatoki, at 2.6 metres the largest in the Kantō. In the Meiji era Engaku-ji became the chief centre of Zen instruction in the Kantō under the abbots Imakita Kōsen and Sōyen Shaku, who taught Daisetz Teitaro Suzuki; Tokimune himself is buried at the thatched Butsunichian, and zazen is still practised publicly in the Butsuden and Kojirin.

Negoro-ji began as an estate in Kii Province granted in 1132 by the retired Emperor Toba to the reformer Kakuban, who from 1131 had headed Shingon on Mount Kōya and made enemies there by trying to reunite the Ōno and Hirosawa branches, to assert Kōya's authority over the metropolitan headquarters at Tō-ji, and to fold Pure Land elements into Shingon orthodoxy through a new rite, the himitsu nembutsu or esoteric nembutsu. He resigned his posts in 1135, and after armed followers of rival factions burned his residence in 1140 he fled south to this mountain, dying here in 1143; his disciple Raiyū (1226 to 1304) moved the Daidenbō-in and Mitsugon-in chapels down from Kōya in 1288 and made Negoro-ji the seat of an independent school, Shingi Shingon or New Shingon. By the late Muromachi period the mountainside had swollen into a religious city of roughly 450 temples and chapels (2,700 by some accounts), controlling estates assessed at 720,000 koku and fielding some 10,000 Negoro-shū soldiers, many carrying the newly introduced matchlock, which made the temple the equal of a major Sengoku daimyō in economic and military might. It had assisted Oda Nobunaga during the Ishiyama Hongan-ji War of 1570 to 1580 and Tokugawa Ieyasu at Komaki and Nagakute in 1584, but it earned the enmity of Toyotomi Hideyoshi, whose invasion of Kii in 1585 left most of the complex in ashes; because Negoro-ji surrendered without resistance, whether the fire was set on Hideyoshi's orders, by the attackers, or by the defenders remains disputed. Rebuilding proceeded under Tokugawa patronage, Ieyasu donating the buildings of Hideyoshi's Shoun-ji after 1615 and the Kishū Tokugawa sustaining the work through the Edo period, so that the 40 metre Daitō, the largest tahōtō pagoda in Japan (begun around 1480, finished around 1547, still pitted with bullet holes from the 1585 attack and a National Treasure since 1899), now stands beside the Daishi-dō of about 1391 on grounds designated a National Historic Site and Place of Scenic Beauty in 2007.

descriptions.value: Founded in 1496, when Rennyo, the great revivalist abbot of Jōdo Shinshū (then commonly called Ikkō-shū), retired to a long slope known as Ōzaka at the mouth of the Yodo River in Settsu Province, on ground that recent archaeology places atop the ruins of the ancient Naniwa imperial palace. His small devotional hall drew followers so quickly that the temple and its surrounding town had reached roughly their final extent by his death three years later, and after the destruction of the Yamashina Mido in 1532 it served as the head temple of the Ikkō sect and the principal fortress of the Ikkō-ikki, the leagues of warrior priests and commoners who opposed samurai rule. Its coastal position made it near impregnable: about a hundred priests patrolled at any given hour, upwards of ten thousand could be summoned to battle by the ringing of a bell, contributions arrived through a system of brokers based in the merchant port of Sakai, and the Mōri clan resupplied the fortress when it was under siege. Oda Nobunaga invested it in 1570 and was held off for eleven years, the longest siege in Japanese history, until Abbot Kōsa (Kennyo) was persuaded to surrender in August 1580, whereupon the entire complex was set aflame, by some accounts from within, to deny Nobunaga any material gain from his victory. Nothing of it remains to visit: three years later Toyotomi Hideyoshi began raising Osaka Castle on the same site.

descriptions.value: The Hongan-ji line began in 1321 at the Ōtani Mausoleum, burial place of Shinran, founder of Jōdo Shinshū, whose great-grandson Kakunyo became its first chief priest and third monshu and dedicated it to the worship of Amida; the present Kyoto compound dates from 1591, when Toyotomi Hideyoshi granted Kennyo this land in reward for his surrender at Ishiyama Hongan-ji. Kennyo's son Kyōnyo, publicly disowned for refusing that surrender, threw his support behind Tokugawa Ieyasu instead and was rewarded with a temple immediately to the east, known from 1603 as Higashi Hongan-ji; in 1619 the government recognised the two as separate congregations, and Nishi Hongan-ji has remained head temple of the Hongwanji-ha. Seven of its structures are designated National Treasures, among them the Goeidō or Founder's Hall of 1636, rebuilt after an earthquake in 1596 and a fire in 1617, which enshrines a wooden image of Shinran and hosts the temple's major ceremonies, and the Amidadō of 1760, the main worship hall, whose altar holds an Amida flanked by portraits of six of the seven Pure Land masters together with images of Shinran's master Hōnen and of Prince Shōtoku. The karamon gate, built for Hideyoshi's Fushimi Castle around 1598 and moved here in 1632 for a planned visit by Tokugawa Iemitsu, is carved so densely with flowers, animals and figures from Chinese legend that it is nicknamed the Higurashi no Mon, the 'all day gate'. Much of the complex survives from the Azuchi-Momoyama and early Edo periods, and in 1994 Nishi Hongan-ji was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List as part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.
