descriptions.value: Higashi Hongan-ji, the Eastern Monastery of the Original Vow, was established in 1602 when Tokugawa Ieyasu divided Jōdo Shinshū in two in order to diminish its power, and it has been the head temple of the Ōtani-ha branch ever since, though the buildings first stood on their present ground only in 1658. Its precinct holds the mausoleum of Shinran, founder of the sect, first constructed in 1272 and relocated several times before reaching this site in 1670. The main halls burned four times during the Edo period: in the Great Tenmei Fire of 1788 (rebuilt 1797), an accidental fire in 1823 (rebuilt 1835), a third in 1858 whose temporary replacements were run up in time for Shinran's 600th memorial service in 1861, and finally the city-wide conflagration caused by the Kinmon incident of 19 July 1864. The Tokugawa shogunate had repeatedly funded the rebuilding, but after 1864 reconstruction waited until 1879, once the fall of the shogunate and the upheaval of the Meiji Restoration had settled; the Goeidō and Amida Hall were completed in 1895 and the remaining buildings by 1911, and these are the halls a visitor sees today. The Goeidō, enshrining an image of Shinran, is among the largest wooden structures in the world at 76 metres long, 58 metres wide and 38 metres high, while the Amida Hall beside it, ornately worked in gold leaf and Meiji-era art, holds images of Amida and of Prince Shōtoku; Kyoto knows the two rival compounds affectionately as Ohigashisan and Onissan, Honorable Mr. East and Honorable Mr. West.

descriptions.value: Byōdō-in, the 'Temple of Equality', began as a country villa built at Uji in 998 for the high-ranking courtier Minamoto no Shigenobu, Minister of the Left; Fujiwara no Michinaga bought the property from the courtier's widow, and Michinaga's son Fujiwara no Yorimichi converted it into a Buddhist temple in 1052. That year was widely believed to mark the first of mappō, the degenerate Latter Day of the Law, and the anxiety it produced turned aristocrats and monks toward the Pure Land of Amida, the devotion the new temple was built to serve. The Amida-dō, completed in 1053 and known from the early Edo period as the Hōō-dō or Phoenix Hall (both for the pair of Chinese phoenixes on its roof and for its outspread wing and tail corridors), stands at the edge of an artificial pond in a Jōdo-shiki garden, the hall facing east so that a worshipper crosses the water toward it as toward the Pure Land itself; within sits Jōchō's gold-leafed cypress Amida, carved in the yosegi technique of hollowed blocks joined from the inside, whose proportions he made canonical. Kusunoki Masashige set fire to the precinct in 1336 while fighting the Ashikaga and the Phoenix Hall is the only original building to survive; from the seventeenth century two sub-temples, Jōdo-in of the Jōdo sect and Saishō-in of the Tendai sect, cooperated to keep the place running, and Byōdō-in remains jointly a Jōdo-shū and Tendai-shū temple. The hall, its Amida, the temple bell, the twenty-six praying bodhisattvas on clouds and the raigō paintings on the doors are all National Treasures, most now displayed in the largely subterranean Hōshōkan Museum opened in 2001; the site was inscribed by UNESCO in 1994 as part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto, and the hall appears on the ten yen coin, its phoenix on the ten thousand yen note.

descriptions.value: Zenkō-ji was founded in the seventh century, before Japanese Buddhism divided into sects, and the town that grew around it became the modern city of Nagano; it is still co-managed by twenty-five priests of the Tendai school and fourteen of the Jōdo-shū, seated respectively at the Daikanjin, residence of the chief priest, and the Daihongan, which houses the nunnery and the high priestess. Its honzon is an image of Amida said to have reached Japan from India by way of the Korean peninsula in the sixth century, in the reign of Emperor Kinmei, and rumoured to be the first Buddhist statue brought to the country; legend holds that the image, having set two clans against one another, was thrown into a canal and recovered by Honda Yoshimitsu, whose name read in the Chinese manner gave the temple its own. That icon is a hibutsu (hidden Buddha) which the temple's commandments forbid anyone to view, the chief priest included, so a substitute image, the Maedachi Honzon, is shown once every six years at the Gokaichō (the most recent showing, put off from 2021 to 2022 by the pandemic, was extended to eighty-eight days to thin the crowds). Copies of the icon proliferated from the end of the Kamakura period, producing "Shin-Zenkō-ji" foundations across the provinces, and in the sixteenth century the temple lay between Uesugi Kenshin, who used it as a base of operations, and Takeda Shingen; an anxious chief abbot founded a replacement Zenkō-ji at what is now Kōfu, and in 1598 Toyotomi Hideyoshi moved the hibutsu to Kyoto and then to Shinano before it returned to Nagano. Visitors pass the Niōmon with its guardian Niō, then the Sanmon and the Kyōzō of 1759, whose octagonal sūtra case of 1694 is turned for merit (both are Important Cultural Properties), to reach the Hon-dō, a National Treasure, below which a wholly dark corridor invites pilgrims to feel for the key to Amida's Western Paradise.

Kiyomizu-dera, properly Otowa-san Kiyomizu-dera, stands on Mount Otowa in the Higashiyama hills and is one of the very few Kyoto temples older than Heian-kyō itself. Its founding legend, preserved in the Kiyomizu-dera Engi and retold in the Konjaku Monogatarishū, has the Kōfuku-ji monk Kenshin (later Enchin) follow a golden stream in 778 to the ascetic Gyōei, from whose sacred tree he carved a Senjū Kannon; two years later the warrior Sakanoue no Tamuramaro, hunting deer on the mountain for his sick wife, was turned to Kannon worship, gave his own residence as the main hall and later prayed here before campaigning against the Emishi. Granted temple land in 805 and imperial recognition as Kita Kannon-ji in 810, it long belonged to the Hossō establishment of Kōfuku-ji and was dragged into that temple's feud with Enryaku-ji, whose warrior monks burned it in 1165; it burned again in the Ōnin War in 1469, when the Ji-sect fundraiser Gan'ami organised the rebuilding, and in all the complex burned nine times before the fire of 1629. The present Hon-dō, a National Treasure, was rebuilt in 1633 with a donation from Tokugawa Iemitsu, and its broad kakezukuri veranda, thrust out over the slope on tall pillars and built without a single nail, gave Japanese the phrase about "jumping off the stage at Kiyomizu" (234 Edo-period jumps were recorded, 85.4 per cent of them survived, and the practice was banned in 1872). Fifteen further structures are Important Cultural Properties, the Otowa waterfall below the hall still sends down three channels of wish-granting water, and the temple, sixteenth stop on the Saigoku Kannon pilgrimage and a Kita-Hossō foundation since its abbot Ōnishi Ryokei broke from the Hossō sect in 1965, lies within the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto World Heritage Site.

Sensō-ji, formally Kinryū-zan Sensō-ji and popularly Asakusa Kannon, is Tokyo's oldest-established temple and is dedicated to Kannon, the bodhisattva of compassion. Legend recorded in the Sensō Engi has the brothers Hinokuma Hamanari and Takenari net a small golden Kannon from the Sumida River in 628, after which their village headman Haji no Nakatomo took vows and turned his house into a temple; in 645 the monk Katsumi rebuilt it and, following a dream, declared the image a hibutsu, which has never since been shown. The temple enters documented history in the Azuma kagami, which records Minamoto no Yoritomo summoning Asakusa carpenters in 1181 to build Tsurugaoka Hachiman-gū and Sensō-ji monks attending Emperor Go-Shirakawa's memorial service in 1192; in 1590 Tokugawa Ieyasu made it an official prayer temple of his shogunate with 500 koku of land, and after fires in 1631 and 1642 Tokugawa Iemitsu paid for a new five-story pagoda in 1648 and main hall in 1649. Under that patronage Asakusa became the pleasure ground of commoner Edo: shops that became the Nakamise were licensed along the approach in 1685 in exchange for cleaning the precinct, street performances filled the "Okuyama" ground behind the hall, and the three licensed Edo theatres moved to the district in 1843 and 1844. Saved from the 1923 Great Kantō earthquake by a bucket brigade, the main hall (a national treasure at the time) and the pagoda were destroyed in the firebombing of 10 March 1945; the hall was rebuilt in 1951 to 1958 and now carries a titanium-tiled roof, the Kaminarimon followed in 1960 with money from Konosuke Matsushita, the Hōzōmon in 1964 and the pagoda in 1973, and the temple, which left the Tendai sect to become independent in 1950, still owns the Heian-period Lotus Sutra set designated a National Treasure.

descriptions.value: Rinnō-ji is the Tendai temple at the heart of Nikkō, established in 766 by the monk Shōdō Shōnin (735 to 817); its isolation deep in the mountains soon drew other monks in search of solitude, and it remains an important base for ascetic training among Tendai monks. Its best-known building, the Sanbutsudō or Three Buddha Hall, enshrines gold-leafed images of Amida, Senju Kannon and Batō Kannon, which are understood as the Buddhist manifestations of Nikkō's three mountain kami worshipped next door at Futarasan Shrine. The temple also administers the Taiyū-in Reibyō, the mausoleum of the third shōgun Tokugawa Iemitsu (1604 to 1651), built in 1653 in gongen-zukuri style; technically a Shinto shrine, it is a designated National Treasure and was praised by the World Heritage Committee as a masterpiece of architecture and decoration. Beside the Sanbutsudō lie the Shōyō-en garden and the Homotsu-den treasure house, which displays about fifty items at a time from a collection of sculpture, painting, calligraphy and scrolls running back to the eighth century, while the temple also holds the Daihatsu nehankyō shūge, a National Treasure commentary on the Nirvana Sutra in fifty-nine handscrolls of Nara and Heian date. Its hibutsu Chinjō Yasha, a yakṣa taken as a manifestation of Vaiśravaṇa and a protector of the state, is unveiled in the Great Goma Hall only once every nine years (most recently on 3 February 2023), and Rinnō-ji, with thirty-seven of its structures designated Important Cultural Properties, forms part of the Shrines and Temples of Nikkō World Heritage Site together with Nikkō Tōshō-gū and Futarasan Shrine.

Fushimi Inari-taisha, the head shrine of the kami Inari, was formally founded in 711 (the Wadō era) by the Hata clan, toraijin immigrants from the Korean Peninsula who had settled Yamashiro Province during the Kofun period and brought continental skills in irrigation, sericulture and sake brewing; the Yamashiro-no-kuni Fudoki attributes its establishment to Hata no Irogu, who is said to have shot an arrow at a rice cake that turned into a white bird and alighted on the peak of Mount Inari. Inari remains above all the kami of rice and agriculture, but the clan's technical expertise and its close ties to the imperial court carried the deity from a private clan tutelary (ujigami) into a national protector of the harvest and of the state, and merchants in time took Inari as the patron of business. The shrine drew imperial patronage in the early Heian period and was among the sixteen shrines to receive Emperor Murakami's heihaku offerings in 965; from 1871 to 1946 it ranked as a Kanpei-taisha, in the first class of government-supported shrines, and it is said today to have as many as 32,000 branch shrines (bunsha) across Japan. The earliest structures of 711 stood on Inariyama and were relocated in 816 at the request of the monk Kūkai, the present main shrine building dates from 1499, and a drawing of 1786 records the two-storey entrance gate as the work of Toyotomi Hideyoshi. Visitors pass the rōmon and the honden and climb some four kilometres of mountain path to the inner shrine (okumiya) and to tens of thousands of privately dedicated rock altars (otsuka), walking beneath roughly 10,000 vermilion torii given by businesses, about 800 of which form the tunnel of the Senbon torii, a votive custom that spread from the Edo period; stone foxes (kitsune), Inari's messengers, hold the key to the rice granary in their mouths.

descriptions.value: Sanzen-in is a Tendai monzeki temple at Ōhara, about an hour north of central Kyoto, founded by the monk Saichō, who introduced Tendai Buddhism to Japan in 804. Monzeki rank placed it among the small number of temples whose head priests were drawn from the imperial family, binding the house directly to the court. Its Heian-period triad of Amida Nyorai flanked by attendants is designated a National Treasure; the Ōjō Gokuraku-in, the oldest building on the grounds, was first raised in 985 and last rebuilt in 1143, and it holds the temple's most valued image, an Amida Buddha attended by Kannon on one side and Seishi on the other. Visitors pass first through the Kyakuden, a guest hall displaying calligraphy and painted sliding doors (fusuma), which opens onto the Shūheki-en garden with its small pond and hill, and then by corridor to the Shinden, where a further Amida stands flanked by Kannon and Fudō Myōō. From the Shinden the temple's best-known view opens across a moss garden studded with small stone figures towards the Ōjō Gokuraku-in among maple and cedar, at its finest in the autumn colours of mid-November; paths beyond lead to later halls, to rows of miniature Kannon donated by visitors, and to a treasure house.

descriptions.value: Myōhō-ji, formally Ryōgonzan Renge-in Myōhō-ji, is a Nichiren temple in the Matsubagayatsu district of Kamakura, the Valley of Pine Needles, where Nichiren is held to have built his hut after coming to what was then the political and cultural centre of the country; by the temple's own records he settled here in 1253 and left for Minobu in 1272. Three temples in the valley (Ankokuron-ji, Chōshō-ji and Myōhō-ji) have contested that honour for centuries, and it was a ruling of the shogunate's courts in 1787 that granted Myōhō-ji the right to call itself the site of the hermitage. The ground was first occupied by a temple called Honkoku-ji, later transferred to Kyoto; Myōhō-ji was rebuilt in 1357 by its fifth chief abbot Nichiei, a natural son of Prince Morinaga, who dedicated it to his father, and it was protected and maintained by the Tokugawa and their vassals throughout the Edo period. Nichiei set two cenotaphs to his parents on the hill behind the main hall, and he and his mother Minami no Ōnkata are buried in the precinct, while Prince Morinaga, imprisoned by the Ashikaga in the cave now within Kamakura-gū and killed in 1335 at the age of 28, lies nearby at Nikaidō. The buildings are all kept closed to the public: a main hall holding a bone fragment revered as a relic of Nichiren and an effigy of Prince Morinaga, the Daigakuden with images of Shaka Nyorai, Katō Kiyomasa and Inari Myōjin, and the Hokkedō or Hall of Scriptures above; the temple's fame today rests on the fifty mossy steps that climb from the Niō gate, which have earned it the nickname Kokedera, the moss temple.

Kumano Nachi Taisha stands amid cedar forest in the Kii Mountains above Nachikatsuura in Wakayama Prefecture, enshrining Fusumi no kami, identified with Izanami no Mikoto, together with other deities. It is one of the three Kumano Sanzan shrines alongside Kumano Hongū Taisha and Kumano Hayatama Taisha, and pilgrims completed the Kumano circuit only by visiting all three, travelling the mountain roads now known collectively as the Kumano Kodō. The site is a clear case of Shintō and Buddhist syncretism (shinbutsu shūgō), the shrine standing beside the temple of Seiganto-ji, while the 133-metre Nachi Falls, worshipped at the nearby Hiryū Shrine, is believed to be inhabited by a kami called Hiryū Gongen. Between the shrine's heiden and Seiganto-ji grows a sacred camphor some 850 years old, said to have been planted by Taira no Shigemori (1138-1179) and girdled with a straw rope (shimenawa) and paper flags to mark it as a kami; its hollow base can be entered, where a small altar receives offerings. The shrine's principal festival is the Nachi-no-Hi Matsuri on 14 July, in which men dressed in white carry six-metre portable shrines and oversized torches whose fire symbolically purifies the waterfall, and Kumano Nachi Taisha is inscribed, with the other Kumano shrines and Kōya-san, in the UNESCO World Heritage Sacred Sites and Pilgrimage Routes in the Kii Mountain Range.

descriptions.value: Nikkō Tōshō-gū (日光東照宮) is the Shinto shrine dedicated to Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the Tokugawa shogunate, whose remains are entombed on the wooded slope above it; it was first built in 1617, while Ieyasu's son Hidetada was shōgun, by the Tokugawa retainer Tōdō Takatora, and was enlarged under the third shōgun, Iemitsu. Its role was as much political as devotional: throughout the Edo period the shogunate mounted stately processions from Edo to the shrine along the Nikkō Kaidō, journeys still reenacted at the spring and autumn festivals known as the processions of a thousand warriors, on a route lined by the cedars of the Cedar Avenue of Nikkō. The decoration is famously dense for a Shinto site: the Yōmeimon (陽明門) carries carvings in deep relief painted in rich colors and bears the nickname higurashi no mon no kei, meaning that one could look at it until sundown and not tire of seeing it; the next gate is the karamon, decorated with white ornaments, and nearby are the sleeping cat (Nemuri-neko) attributed to Hidari Jingorō and, on the stable of the sacred horses, the three wise monkeys who hear, speak and see no evil, a motif derived from a passage in the Analects. The five-storey pagoda, donated by a daimyō in 1650, burned down and was rebuilt in 1818; its storeys stand in ascending order for earth, water, fire, wind and aether, and its central shinbashira pillar hangs from chains to minimize damage from earthquakes. Visitors today climb hundreds of stone steps through the cryptomeria forest to Ieyasu's grave, where a torii bearing calligraphy attributed to Emperor Go-Mizunoo stands before the bronze urn holding his remains; forty-two of the shrine's structures are inscribed, together with Futarasan Shrine and Rinnō-ji, as the UNESCO World Heritage Site Shrines and Temples of Nikkō, five of them National Treasures of Japan and three more Important Cultural Properties (two swords held by the shrine are also National Treasures).

Hōryū-ji stands at Ikaruga, on the plain west of Nara, and it is the oldest surviving Buddhist complex in Japan. Prince Shōtoku and Empress Suiko founded it in 607, dedicating it to Yakushi Nyorai, the Buddha of healing, in memory of Shōtoku's father. Its full name, Hōryū Gakumonji or Learning Temple of the Flourishing Law, records what it was for: the complex served as a seminary as well as a monastery, one of the doors through which continental Buddhist learning entered Japan.

According to the Nihon Shoki the original buildings burned down after a lightning strike in 670. The temple was rebuilt on a slightly shifted alignment, probably finished around 711, and it is that rebuilding that survives. The kondō, or golden hall, and the five-story pagoda beside it are generally recognised as the oldest wooden buildings anywhere in the world. Tree ring dating puts the felling of the pagoda's central pillar at 594, and some kondō timbers before 670, which suggests the replacement hall was already going up when the fire came.

Hōryū-ji was counted among the Seven Great Temples of Nara and was long tied to the Hossō school. From the twelfth century it became the centre of the cult of Prince Shōtoku, venerated there as an incarnation of Kannon, and the Shōryō-e memorial service for him is still held. The Meiji settlement stripped the temple of land and income; it went over to Shingon for a time before returning to Hossō, and it is now the head temple of its own Shōtoku school.

A fire during repair work in January 1949 gutted much of the kondō's ground floor and its Asuka period murals. The restoration finished in 1954 kept perhaps fifteen to twenty percent of the seventh century fabric, and the wall paintings on view today are reproductions of 1967; the date of the fire is now Japan's fire prevention day for cultural properties. The temple holds over 180 National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties, among them the Shaka triad, the Kudara Kannon and the octagonal Yumedono of 739. In 1993 it became, with nearby Hokki-ji, Japan's first UNESCO World Heritage listing.

Yakushi-ji was commissioned in 680 by Emperor Tenmu, who vowed to build it as a prayer for the recovery of his consort from a serious illness. She outlived him. Tenmu died in 686, she took the throne herself as Empress Jitō, and she saw the temple through to completion at Fujiwara-kyō, the capital of the day, around 698. The name comes from its principal image, Yakushi Nyorai, the Medicine Buddha, which suits the circumstances of the vow. When the court moved to Heijō-kyō (Nara) in 710 the temple followed, traditionally in 718, and it took its place among the Seven Great Temples of Nara, the cluster of state-sponsored houses that formed the religious backbone of the Nara court. Excavation of the Fujiwara site in the 1990s complicated the simple story of a move: it now appears both temples may have stood at once, and the older site is known as Moto Yakushi-ji, the original Yakushi-ji.

Yakushi-ji became one of the two centres of the Hossō school, the Japanese form of the Chinese Faxiang tradition of consciousness-only philosophy, and it remains a head temple of that school today alongside Kōfuku-ji. Its ground plan, a Golden Hall flanked by two matching three-storey pagodas, is distinctive enough that architectural historians call it the Yakushi-ji style.

Fire has cost the temple most of its fabric. The complex burned in 973 and the main hall was lost again in 1528 during the wars of the sixteenth century. What survives from the Nara period is the East Pagoda, finished in 730. It stands 34 metres tall and has three storeys that read as six, because a mokoshi or skirt roof is tucked beneath each main roof. It is a National Treasure and the only eighth-century building on the site, and it was taken apart for repair between 2012 and 2018 after its central pillar decayed. Everything else is modern: the Golden Hall dates from 1976, the West Pagoda from 1981, the central gate from 1984 and the side gates from 1995. The bronze Yakushi Triad inside the Golden Hall is among the finest sculpture to survive from the Hakuhō period, with Tang Chinese influence plain in its full, naturalistic figures. Yakushi-ji was inscribed by UNESCO in 1998 as part of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara.

Tōshōdai-ji was founded in 759 by Ganjin (Chinese Jianzhen, 688 to 763), a master of the vinaya from Yangzhou whom Japanese envoys had begged to come and put ordination on a proper footing. Japan then had no fully qualified ordination masters, so men took the robe privately, often to escape tax and labour service, and the court wanted the monastic rule enforced. Ganjin tried to cross for eleven years and failed five times, losing his sight along the way, and reached Kyushu only in 753 on the sixth attempt, aged sixty-six. In 754 he ordained the retired Emperor Shōmu, Empress Dowager Kōmyō and the reigning Empress Kōken at Tōdai-ji, where Japan's first ordination platform was built the following year. In 759 the court granted him the site of the vacant mansion of Prince Niitabe in the western half of Heijō-kyō, and he turned it into a private school of the precepts, first called Tō-ritsu-shōdai, a training hall for the Tang vinaya. It became the head temple of the Ritsu school, the branch of Japanese Buddhism founded on monastic discipline itself rather than on a body of doctrine. Observance lapsed in the later Heian period and the temple decayed; the monk Kakujō revived it from 1244 as part of the Kamakura movement to restore the precepts, and a fire in 1802 destroyed the five-storeyed east pagoda. What survives is exceptional. The kondō, whose timbers include cypress felled in 781, is the only Nara-period golden hall still standing, and its open seven-bay portico of eight heavy columns fronts a National Treasure Vairocana in dry lacquer backed by a halo of hundreds of small Buddhas; it was dismantled and reassembled in a full repair between 2000 and 2009. The kōdō behind it is the East Assembly Hall of the Heijō Palace, moved here about 760 and reroofed for temple use, the sole surviving building of Nara palace architecture. Ganjin's seated portrait in dry lacquer, made around the time of his death in 763, is the oldest portrait sculpture in Japan and is shown to the public for only a few days each June. The temple has formed part of the UNESCO World Heritage site Historic Monuments of Ancient Nara since 1998.

Chūson-ji stands on a wooded ridge above the Kitakami River at Hiraizumi, in what is now southern Iwate. The temple's own tradition dates its founding to 850 and credits Ennin, the third head of the Tendai school, though the historian George Sansom put the real foundation much later, with Fujiwara no Kiyohira in 1095. What is certain is that in the early twelfth century Kiyohira, founder of the Northern Fujiwara, built the site up on an enormous scale. He had lived through the Former Nine Years War and the Latter Three Years' War and lost his family in them, and the temple was raised to quiet the souls of everyone who had died on either side. The Azuma Kagami, the Kamakura shogunate's own chronicle, describes more than forty halls and pagodas and over three hundred monks' residences. Kiyohira's son Motohira went on to build Mōtsū-ji nearby, and his grandson Hidehira added Muryōkō-in, so that for close to a century Hiraizumi flourished as the seat of an effectively independent northern power.

That ended in 1189, when Minamoto no Yoritomo destroyed the Northern Fujiwara. Chūson-ji survived the war but fell into decline, and a fire in 1337 took most of the buildings. Only two structures from Kiyohira's temple came through: the sutra repository and, above all, the Konjikidō of 1124. It is a small hall, roughly five and a half metres to a side and eight metres tall, covered in gold leaf inside and out and finished with mother of pearl inlay, lacquer, metalwork and painting. Under its three altars lie the mummified bodies of the first three Fujiwara lords, together with the severed head of the fourth, Yasuhira, killed in 1189. It was the first building in Japan to be designated a National Treasure. The temple was partly restored in the Edo period by the Date lords of Sendai, and Matsuo Bashō stopped here on the journey recorded in Oku no Hosomichi.

Several thousand National Treasures and Important Cultural Properties survive at Chūson-ji, among them the Chūson-ji sutras written in gold and silver ink. The Konjikidō, once open to the weather and first roofed over in 1288, was dismantled and restored between 1962 and 1968 and now sits behind glass inside a concrete shelter of 1965. The precinct became a Special Historic Site in 1979 and was inscribed by UNESCO in June 2011 as part of the Historic Monuments and Sites of Hiraizumi. It remains the head temple of the Tendai school in the Tōhoku region.

Eihei-ji is the mountain monastery in which Sōtō Zen took its Japanese form. Dōgen had studied in Song China and came home in 1227 convinced that seated meditation, zazen, was not a technique for reaching enlightenment but enlightenment itself. His temple in Kyoto attracted hostility from the entrenched Tendai establishment on Mount Hiei, and in 1243 he accepted an invitation from his patron, the warrior Hatano Yoshishige, to move to Yoshishige's estate at Shihi in Echizen province, deep in a wooded valley in what is now Fukui Prefecture. He built a temple there in 1244 and named it Daibutsu-ji, changing the name to Eihei-ji in 1246 after the Chinese era in which Buddhism was said to have first reached China. The remoteness was the point. Dōgen wanted a community out of reach of the capital and its politics, living under a minutely regulated rule in which cooking, washing and sleeping counted as practice just as much as sitting did. He died in 1253, and it was his successors, above all Keizan Jōkin two generations later, who carried the school into the provinces, where it grew into the largest Buddhist denomination in Japan by number of temples.

Eihei-ji itself was often poor and repeatedly destroyed, burning in fighting in 1340 and again in 1473 during the Ōnin War. Its status was settled only in 1615, when a Tokugawa decree recognised it as one of the two head temples, daihonzan, of Sōtō alongside Sōji-ji, a rank the two have shared, not always comfortably, ever since. Nothing from Dōgen's own time survives above ground. The seventy-odd buildings that climb the hillside today, linked by roofed stairways and corridors, are Edo period and later. The two-storeyed Sanmon gate of 1749 is the oldest, the Hattō or dharma hall dates from 1843, and the Buddha hall and monks' hall were rebuilt in 1902. Nineteen of these structures are designated national Important Cultural Properties, and the temple holds a National Treasure in Dōgen's own manuscript of the Fukan zazengi, his short universal recommendation of zazen. Eihei-ji has no World Heritage listing, but it is still a working training monastery with a resident community of novices, and it remains the yardstick against which Sōtō practice is measured.

Sōji-ji is one of the two head temples (daihonzan) of Sōtō Zen, the larger of Japan's two main Zen schools, and for almost all of its history it stood not in Yokohama but here on the Noto peninsula. The site began as Morooka-dera, an esoteric temple traditionally credited to the monk Gyōki in about 740 and attached to a Shinto shrine. In 1321 its incumbent, Jōken, made it over to Keizan Jōkin, revered in Sōtō as its great patriarch, who reorganised it as a Zen monastery and renamed it Sōji-ji. Keizan drew up its rule in 1324, and his successor Gasan Jōseki turned the place into an engine of expansion. Five sub-temples, each headed by one of Gasan's leading disciples, took turns supplying the abbot in a rotation that lasted until 1870, and monks trained here were sent out into the provinces, where they converted small village chapels into full Sōtō temples. That is why Sōtō grew into a rural, nationwide school rather than a metropolitan one, and why most Sōtō temples in Japan descend from this line. A shogunal survey of the 1740s counted 16,391 branch temples under Sōji-ji. It argued for centuries with Eihei-ji in Echizen over which was senior; the Tokugawa settled the quarrel in 1615 by recognising both as head temples, and Sōji-ji received 1,000 ryō and the status of a shogunal prayer temple, followed by 400 koku of land in 1657 under the Kaga domain.

The temple burned in the fighting of 1570 and was rebuilt under the Maeda, then burned almost to nothing again in 1898. That fire prompted the move: in 1911 the head temple was transferred to Tsurumi in Yokohama, and the Noto original was renamed Sōji-ji Soin, the founding temple. What stands there today is largely the reconstruction of 1905 and after, including the monks' hall of 1930 and the great gate of 1932, though Keizan's mausoleum of 1693 and the sutra repository survived the fire. Earthquakes have treated it worse than any war. The Noto quake of 2007 damaged all thirty buildings and repairs were only completed in 2021; on 1 January 2024 much of the seven-hall precinct and its connecting corridors collapsed. In December 2024 sixteen of its buildings were designated national Important Cultural Properties, and the restoration programme announced in 2025 is expected to run until about 2034.

Daigo-ji was founded in 874, when Shōbō, a disciple of Kūkai, climbed Mount Kasatori southeast of the capital, found a spring of holy water there, and enshrined images of Juntei and Nyoirin Kannon that he had carved himself. The name Daigo means the last and finest of the five flavours drawn from milk, a Buddhist metaphor for the highest teaching, and it attached itself to both the spring and the temple. What began as a mountain hermitage became an imperial foundation under Emperor Daigo, who made it his prayer temple and whose name it shares. A Yakushi hall went up in 907 and a Shaka hall in 926, these on the flat ground below rather than on the summit, so the complex settled into two halves: the upper precinct, Kami-Daigo, still an hour's climb up the mountain, and the lower precinct, Shimo-Daigo, at its foot. The five-storey pagoda was vowed in 931 for the repose of Emperor Daigo and completed only in 951, twenty years later.

Daigo-ji is the head temple of the Shingon Daigo-ha, one of the principal branches of esoteric Shingon Buddhism, and its abbots ranked among the most powerful clergy in Kyoto. That standing did not protect it. In the Ōnin War of the later fifteenth century Shimo-Daigo burned, and the pagoda of 951 was the one building left upright. The revival came from Toyotomi Hideyoshi, who in 1598 staged the Daigo no hanami, a spectacular cherry blossom party for which he rebuilt the Sanbō-in subtemple and laid out its garden. In the same works he had a late Heian main hall brought up from Kii Province and re-erected as the present Kondō.

The pagoda of 951 survives and is the oldest wooden building in Kyoto Prefecture. The Kondō, the Yakushi-dō and the Seiryū-gū haiden are National Treasures alongside it, as is the main drawing room of Sanbō-in; the Sanbō-in garden is designated both a Special Historic Site and a Special Place of Scenic Beauty. The temple holds roughly 150,000 treasures, many of them National Treasures or Important Cultural Properties, a selection of which is shown in its Reihōkan museum. Daigo-ji was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 1994 as one of the seventeen components of the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto. It is still the eleventh station of the Saigoku Kannon pilgrimage, although the Juntei hall that held that station was destroyed by lightning in 2008 and its image moved down to Shimo-Daigo.

Ninna-ji was begun in 886 on the order of Emperor Kōkō, who died before it was finished, and completed in 888 by his son Emperor Uda, who renamed it after the Ninna era. Its first head priest was a Tendai monk, Yūsen, but in 899 Uda took holy orders at the temple and the following year received Shingon initiation at Tō-ji, after which a Shingon abbot was installed and the temple has been Shingon ever since. In 904 the retired emperor built himself quarters called the Omuro to the south-west of the grounds and lived there as a monk. That gave the temple its character and its nickname: it was known as the Omuro Gosho, the Omuro Palace, and from the eleventh century, when a son of Emperor Sanjō was placed over the abbot, it became the foremost of the monzeki temples, those headed by princes of the imperial house. Only two men who were not of imperial blood ever led it. The line of princely abbots ran until 1867, when the thirtieth renounced his vows and became Prince Komatsu, and for nearly nine centuries it bound the Shingon school directly to the court.

The complex burned in the Ōnin War in 1467, though the monks had already carried the founding Amida triad to safety, and the community sheltered elsewhere for well over a century. Rebuilding came with Tokugawa backing: in 1634 the abbot Prince Kakushin won the shogun Iemitsu's consent, and because the Kyoto Imperial Palace was being renewed at the same time, several of its halls were dismantled and re-erected here, the work finishing in 1646. The Kondō is therefore the palace Shishinden of 1613 turned into a Buddhist hall, and it is a National Treasure as the best surviving example of early modern shinden-zukuri architecture. The five-storey pagoda of 1644, the Niōmon, the Kannon-dō, the revolving sutra repository and ten more Edo structures are Important Cultural Properties; the residential palace quarters burned again in 1887 and were rebuilt in 1914. Among the temple's treasures are the Thirty-Volume Sutras that Kūkai brought back from Tang China, partly in his own hand. Ninna-ji remains the head temple of the Omuro school of Shingon, its grove of low, late-flowering Omuro cherries is a designated Place of Scenic Beauty, and it was inscribed by UNESCO in 1994 among the Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto.
